claims.claim: Rosebury holds that Tolkien opens passages in plain modern language and modulates into a higher register only where the narrative touches ancient or magical history.
claims.source: Wikipedia, 'Tolkien's prose style' (citing Rosebury 2003)
claims.quote: modulating into a higher register to deal with echoes

claims.claim: Turner argues Tolkien assigns discrete linguistic registers to different peoples: simple and modern for Hobbits, more archaic for Dwarves, Elves and the Rohirrim.
claims.source: Wikipedia, 'Tolkien's prose style' (citing Turner 2020/2022)
claims.quote: discrete linguistic registers for different characters, peoples

claims.claim: Turner's Companion chapter abstract states that stylistic features become a means of distinguishing characters and their different cultural and ethical outlooks, with local and temporal colour supplied by intertextual references to older literatures.
claims.source: Turner 2022, 'Style and Intertextual Echoes', A Companion to J. R. R. Tolkien (abstract via OpenAlex)

claims.claim: Shippey holds that the Hobbits' modern idiom lets them mediate between the modern reader and the heroic, archaic world of the epic.
claims.source: Wikipedia, 'Tolkien's prose style' (citing Shippey 2005)

claims.claim: Shippey reads 'The Council of Elrond', roughly fifteen thousand words consisting entirely of talk, as a tour de force in which each of many speakers is given a distinct idiom.
claims.source: 'An Analysis of Scholarship on Tolkien: The Council of Elrond' (student synthesis of Shippey)

claims.claim: Shippey shows Elrond's archaism is grammatical as well as lexical, marked by -eth verb endings such as 'seemeth' and 'fadeth' and by inverted word order, signalling his great age.
claims.source: 'An Analysis of Scholarship on Tolkien: The Council of Elrond' (synthesis of Shippey)
claims.quote: old -eth verb endings

claims.claim: Shippey states that Elrond's archaism is consistent and achieved not just by vocabulary but also by grammar.
claims.source: Tolkien: Medieval and Modern blog, 'To Make a Soul' (quoting Shippey)
claims.quote: achieved not just by vocabulary...but also by grammar

claims.claim: Rosebury notes the Dwarves are characterised by curt speech built from short, broken sentences and apposition.
claims.source: Tolkien: Medieval and Modern blog, 'Tolkien's Use of Poetry and Prose' (citing Rosebury)
claims.quote: short, broken sentences and apposition

claims.claim: In Shippey's reading Boromir uses inverted constructions close to Elrond's idiom, while Aragorn in the same scene speaks colloquially.
claims.source: 'An Analysis of Scholarship on Tolkien: The Council of Elrond' (synthesis of Shippey)
claims.quote: inverted constructions

claims.claim: Aragorn's speech register shifts with situation, colloquial among hobbits and formal in high settings, a high/low alternation the essay likens to Auerbach's sermo humilis.
claims.source: Tolkien: Medieval and Modern blog, 'Sublimis and Humilis; Aragorn and Strider'
claims.quote: His manner of speech changes directly with the situation

claims.claim: Saruman's duplicity is conveyed through politically minded, abstract modern speech.
claims.source: Tolkien: Medieval and Modern blog, 'To Make a Soul'
claims.quote: politically minded, abstract manners of speech

claims.claim: Tolkien imagined the Rohirrim speaking the Common Speech more slowly and deliberately because it was their second language.
claims.source: Tolkien: Medieval and Modern blog, 'To Make a Soul' (citing Tolkien's letter to Tiller)
claims.quote: much slower and more deliberate

claims.claim: Rosebury identifies three types of Orc dialogue keyed to rank; Grishnákh speaks like a melodrama villain while Gorbag uses grumbling twentieth-century bureaucratic speech.
claims.source: Wikipedia, 'Tolkien's prose style' (citing Rosebury 2003)
claims.quote: three types of Orc-dialogue for different ranks

claims.claim: Vaninskaya reads the Orcs' speech as the twentieth-century idiom of soldiers, functionaries and minor officials.
claims.source: Wikipedia, 'Tolkien's prose style' (citing Vaninskaya 2020)

claims.claim: Rosebury describes Gollum's extraordinary idiolect of obsessive repetition and infantile whining; the translation literature adds ungrammatical syntax, 'pocketses' plurals and I/we confusion.
claims.source: Wikipedia, 'Tolkien's prose style' (citing Rosebury 2003)
claims.quote: obsessive repetition, infantile whining

claims.claim: Kullmann and Siepmann find all eight members of the Fellowship clearly distinguished by their style of speech.
claims.source: Wikipedia, 'Tolkien's prose style' (citing Kullmann & Siepmann 2021)
claims.quote: eight members clearly distinguished by style of speech

claims.claim: Shippey holds that Tolkien understood archaism technically enough to switch it on and off at will, as he could modern colloquialism, and that this linguistic control is among his least appreciated abilities.
claims.source: Salka Wind blog, 'Language, Thought, and Worldviews in Tolkien's Writing' (quoting Shippey)
claims.quote: could switch it on and off at will

claims.claim: In Letter 171 Tolkien rejects the 'tushery' charge, arguing real archaic English is terser than modern English, which is looser and full of little empty words.
claims.source: Salka Wind blog (quoting Tolkien, Letter 171)
claims.quote: looser, more full of little 'empty' words

claims.claim: Tolkien claims archaic English offers word orders that are terser, more vivid and sometimes nobler, and that a king speaking modern English would not have had those thoughts.
claims.source: Salka Wind blog (quoting Tolkien, Letter 171)
claims.quote: terser, more vivid, and sometimes nobler

claims.claim: Walker argues Tolkien uses only a few genuinely archaic words, and those rarely; the archaic effect comes mainly from syntax.
claims.source: Wikipedia, 'Tolkien's prose style' (citing Walker 2009)
claims.quote: only a few actually archaic words, used rarely

claims.claim: Walker holds that the Riders of Rohan are given Anglo-Saxon syntactic patterns and a diction that is stirring, alliteratively stately and stern.
claims.source: Wikipedia, 'Tolkien's prose style' (citing Walker 2009)
claims.quote: stirring, alliteratively stately

claims.claim: The Rohirrim's speech carries actual Old English words and phrases such as éored, dwimmerlaik and mearas, and the Dwarves' speech is archaic, blunt and proverbial.
claims.source: Wikipedia, 'Tolkien's prose style'

claims.claim: Wilton catalogues Old English embedded in the prose: 'Westu Théoden hál', dwimmerlaik (dweomer + -lác), the hobbit words mathom and smial (smygel), and names like Orthanc and Dwarrowdelf.
claims.source: Wordorigins.org, 'Old English in LoTR' (David Wilton)

claims.claim: Turner's example of fronting, placing the object before the verb, is 'Weapons they have laid at your doors', a construction he notes cannot be reproduced in French and is unmarked in German.
claims.source: Wikipedia, 'Translating The Lord of the Rings' (citing Turner)
claims.quote: Weapons they have laid at your doors

claims.feature: Old English to Modern English mapping
claims.claim: Shippey explains that Tolkien rendered Rohirric as Old English so that its relation to Westron mirrors Old English's relation to Modern English.
claims.source: Wikipedia, 'Translating The Lord of the Rings' (citing Shippey)

claims.claim: Siepmann's corpus study finds the reader's impression of archaicity has three lexical causes: overuse of nineteenth-century fiction words, avoidance of modern-world words, and dense coinages, unusual grammar and rare or obsolescent words.
claims.source: Siepmann, 'Tolkien as a stylist: a corpus-based investigation' (CL2017, Birmingham)
claims.quote: three simple lexical causes

claims.claim: Key words shared with a 30-million-word nineteenth-century fiction corpus cluster in landscape, position/direction, warfare, and descriptive verbs and adjectives, many obsolescent when Tolkien wrote.
claims.source: Siepmann, 'Tolkien as a stylist' (CL2017)
claims.quote: whither, thither, thence, whence, upwards, yonder, afar

claims.claim: Tolkien borrows words such as valour, valiant and corslet from his own Beowulf translation and stretches them to wider uses than Old or Middle English allowed.
claims.source: Siepmann, 'Tolkien as a stylist' (CL2017)
claims.quote: Branched lightning smote down upon the eastward hills

claims.claim: Modern core-vocabulary key words (they, big, wake, smoke) are used in nineteenth-century grammatical patterns, e.g. 'smoke' with an indefinite article.
claims.source: Siepmann, 'Tolkien as a stylist' (CL2017)
claims.quote: a black smoke swirled in the air

claims.claim: Tolkien follows modernist tendencies in his heavy use of manner-laden descriptive verbs such as clutch, cower, flicker, gleam, glint, loom, plod and stride.
claims.source: Siepmann, 'Tolkien as a stylist' (CL2017)
claims.quote: abundant use of descriptive verbs

claims.claim: Words key only to Tolkien (fastness, sheath, lore-masters, gaffer, wolf-riders, yesteryear, yuledays, along, among, outwards) are rare rather than archaic but together create an atmosphere of medievalism.
claims.source: Siepmann, 'Tolkien as a stylist' (CL2017)
claims.quote: atmosphere of medievalism or otherworldliness

claims.claim: Tolkien prefers the most homely collocations but uses everyday adjectives like 'great' with peril, deeds, trees, halls, shadow and smoke at densities beyond nineteenth-century fiction.
claims.source: Siepmann, 'Tolkien as a stylist' (CL2017)
claims.quote: marked preference for the most homely collocations

claims.claim: Key semantic domains for entire/maximum, loud, hot, and long/tall/wide support the hypothesis that Tolkien tends toward hyperbole, while dense plant vocabulary (elm-tree, alder, rowan, hemlock) supplies circumstantial realism.
claims.source: Siepmann, 'Tolkien as a stylist' (CL2017)
claims.quote: Tolkien tends to resort to hyperbole

claims.claim: Siepmann concludes the prose deploys several centuries of linguistic development, putting old words to new uses and vice versa, making Tolkien a linguistic postmodernist.
claims.source: Siepmann, 'Tolkien as a stylist' (CL2017)
claims.quote: he is a linguistic postmodernist

claims.claim: The published chapter abstract states the style relies heavily on the nineteenth-century novel and Tolkien's Beowulf translation, with archaic verb forms, high-frequency along/among/dark/deep/fell/great/long, and collocations mixing archaic and modern registers.
claims.source: Kullmann & Siepmann 2021, 'Tolkien as a Stylist: Key Words and Key Collocations' (Springer chapter abstract)
claims.quote: several centuries' worth of linguistic developments

claims.claim: Lee reports Kullmann and Siepmann's finding that LOTR shares about twice as many key words with nineteenth-century fiction as with late twentieth-century fiction.
claims.source: Lee 2022, 'Where many paths and errands meet: A Close Reading of The Lord of the Rings' (ORA PDF)
claims.quote: around twice as many key words with nineteenth-century fiction

claims.claim: In the Siege of Gondor passage Lee lists real English words fallen from use that feel archaic: hardiest, wreck, slain, foe, thrice, asunder, riven, steadfast, abyss, behold.
claims.source: Lee 2022, close reading (ORA PDF)

claims.claim: Lee finds the most common syntactic device in the passage is fronting of the object, often to pick up something named in the previous sentence.
claims.source: Lee 2022, close reading (ORA PDF)
claims.quote: the object is moved to the beginning

claims.claim: Lee identifies delayed adjectives ('the orcs innumerable', 'a mouth unseen') and inversion with delayed subject as recurrent devices.
claims.source: Lee 2022, close reading (ORA PDF)
claims.quote: In rode the Lord of the Nazgûl

claims.claim: Lee argues inverted syntax combined with archaic lexis evokes older books including the Bible and produces delay and suspense.
claims.source: Lee 2022, close reading (ORA PDF)
claims.quote: the inverted syntax creates delay and suspense

claims.claim: Manuscript evidence shows Tolkien revising sentences to add alliteration, replacing 'like thunder' with 'and rattled' after 'drums rolled'.
claims.source: Lee 2022, close reading (ORA PDF)
claims.quote: seeing the further opportunity for alliteration

claims.claim: Lee shows from typescripts that Tolkien deliberately condensed the climactic prose into short sentences piled one on another, matching Kullmann and Siepmann's 'short, stark sentences' of the epic mode.
claims.source: Lee 2022, close reading (ORA PDF)
claims.quote: Tolkien deliberately condensed the prose

claims.claim: Lee traces medieval-poetic devices of variation (magnifying a character by renaming) and repetition into the prose, e.g. the triple 'Horns, horns, horns' with identity withheld to the final sentence.
claims.source: Lee 2022, close reading (ORA PDF)
claims.quote: Horns, horns, horns

claims.claim: Narratorial 'Behold!' and 'Lo!' reflect biblical semantics mid-sentence rather than the poem-opening Old English 'Hwæt!', a reading Lee credits to Rosebury; 'thrice' appears 9 times in The Silmarillion and 14 more in LOTR for archaic tone.
claims.source: Lee 2022, close reading (ORA PDF)

claims.claim: Shippey (2005, p. 245), as reported by Lee, notes in the Pelennor scene touches of alliteration, old-fashioned semantics and a simple monosyllabic style.
claims.source: Lee 2022, close reading (ORA PDF), citing Shippey
claims.quote: a simple, monosyllabic style

claims.claim: Lee, following Kullmann and Siepmann, describes LOTR's narrator as omnipresent and heterodiegetic, less intrusive than The Hobbit's, ranging over the battlefield with the Old English poet's freedom from space and time.
claims.source: Lee 2022, close reading (ORA PDF)
claims.quote: does not take part in the story

claims.claim: Lee cites Turner (2014) proposing four areas for assessing LOTR's style: registers given to characters, an asymmetrical stylistic arch, semantic archaisms, and syntactic archaisms.
claims.source: Lee 2022, close reading (ORA PDF), citing Turner
claims.quote: Asymmetrical stylistic arch

claims.claim: Lee reports that Drout's 2004 Tolkien Studies article observed repetition, mirroring and non-standard sentence structure as deliberate stylistic effects.
claims.source: Lee 2022, close reading (ORA PDF), citing Drout 2004
claims.quote: repetition and mirroring, and non-standard sentence structure

claims.claim: Drout argues the prose carries meaning beyond the literal text through strategic syntactic ambiguity ('pinnacles or pillars'), apo koinou constructions, deliberate archaisms like 'thrawn', and recurring imagery such as 'grey curtains' that builds a myth feel.
claims.source: Drout, 'How to critique Tolkien's prose style' (Wormtalk and Slugspeak, 2007)
claims.quote: beyond those of the literal text

claims.claim: Drout and Wynne judge the biggest failing of Tolkien criticism to be its lack of discussion of sentence-level writing, word choice and syntax, crediting Shippey, Rosebury, Flieger and Thomas as exceptions.
claims.source: Drout & Wynne, Envoi 9.2 (2000), via ORA
claims.quote: his sentence-level writing, his word choice and syntax

claims.claim: Stimpson (1969) charged that Tolkien shuns ordinary diction and wrenches syntax, inventing 'To an eyot he came' as an example.
claims.source: Wikipedia, 'Tolkien's prose style'
claims.quote: shun[s] ordinary diction, he also wrenches syntax

claims.claim: Rosebury answers Stimpson item by item, locating the three real uses of 'eyot' and arguing their syntax is unexceptional twentieth-century English that Hemingway could have written.
claims.source: Wikipedia, 'Tolkien's prose style' (citing Rosebury)

claims.claim: Rosebury shows Tolkien favouring plain descriptive phrasal verbs 'have on' and 'get off' over the more literary 'wear' and 'dismount', and rejects unsupported charges of archaising and wrenched syntax.
claims.source: Wikipedia, 'Tolkien: A Cultural Phenomenon'
claims.quote: a certain sensuous precision, distinctive of Tolkien

claims.claim: Rosebury reads the Witch-king passage as making effective use of inversion together with assonance and alliteration to produce a powerfully musical sentence.
claims.source: Wikipedia, 'Tolkien's prose style' (citing Rosebury)
claims.quote: powerfully musical sentence

claims.claim: Turner characterises the base style as paratactic, sentences without subordinate clauses or causal conjunctions, with repeated 'and'.
claims.source: Wikipedia, 'Tolkien's prose style' (citing Turner)

claims.claim: Kullmann and Siepmann define the epic register in LOTR by archaic diction, parataxis, plentiful imagery and poetic description, and count 45 to 50 embedded stories told by 23 narrators.
claims.source: Wikipedia, 'Tolkien's prose style' (citing Kullmann & Siepmann 2021)
claims.quote: archaic diction, parataxis, plentiful imagery

claims.claim: Rosebury traces Tolkien's development from an early sustained archaism modelled on William Morris to the mature intimate paternal storytelling style of LOTR.
claims.source: Tolkien: Medieval and Modern blog, 'Tolkien's Use of Poetry and Prose' (citing Rosebury)
claims.quote: a sustained archaism

claims.claim: Le Guin (as summarised) credits the prose with a simple timelessness that avoids both thee/thou archaism and modern slang; Sperling adds that Elrond stays consistently archaic while Aragorn can be wholly colloquial.
claims.source: Tolkien: Medieval and Modern blog, 'A Hobbit Book: The Simplicity of Style'
claims.quote: simple timelessness

claims.claim: Le Guin counted stresses and finds Tolkien's prose runs at the normal narrative ratio of one stress per two to four syllables, rising toward poetry's one-in-two in intense passages.
claims.source: Le Guin, 'Rhythmic Pattern in The Lord of the Rings' (The Wave in the Mind, PDF)
claims.quote: one stress every two to four syllables

claims.claim: Le Guin insists the prose remains irregular and cannot be scanned, the sole exception being Tom Bombadil, whose speech is verse printed as prose with an infectious beat picked up by Goldberry and Frodo.
claims.source: Le Guin, 'Rhythmic Pattern in The Lord of the Rings'
claims.quote: it is irregular, it can't be scanned

claims.claim: Le Guin finds the speech of Elves and noble folk such as Aragorn has a dignified, stately gait without a regular stress-beat, and Théoden only occasionally drops into iambics.
claims.source: Le Guin, 'Rhythmic Pattern in The Lord of the Rings'
claims.quote: dignified, often stately gait, but not a regular stress-beat

claims.claim: Le Guin describes the narrative in passages of epic action as moving in balanced cadences with a majestic sweep reminiscent of epic poetry while remaining pure prose.
claims.source: Le Guin, 'Rhythmic Pattern in The Lord of the Rings'
claims.quote: balanced cadences in passages of epic action

claims.claim: Le Guin identifies the rhythm shaping the whole narrative as the simplest possible, two beats of stress and release, a walking gait, a trochaic alternation contemporaries found simplistic.
claims.source: Le Guin, 'Rhythmic Pattern in The Lord of the Rings'
claims.quote: as simple as a rhythm can be: two beats

claims.claim: Scanning 'Fog on the Barrow-downs', Le Guin found each of a set of polarities (darkness/daylight, resting/traveling, confusion/clarity, menace/ease, imprisonment/freedom, fear/courage) reversed three or four times in the chapter.
claims.source: Le Guin, 'Rhythmic Pattern in The Lord of the Rings'
claims.quote: a positive/negative binary pattern of alternation or reversal

claims.claim: Le Guin notes directionality is important throughout the book, with up and hilltops usually more fortunate than down and valleys.
claims.source: Le Guin, 'Rhythmic Pattern in The Lord of the Rings'
claims.quote: Directionality is extremely important

claims.claim: Le Guin holds the chapter is one beat in the book's rhythm and that the structure is both journeylike and architectural, built by repetition, semirepetition, suggestion, foreshadowing, recollection, echo and reversal.
claims.source: Le Guin, 'Rhythmic Pattern in The Lord of the Rings'
claims.quote: both journeylike and architectural

claims.claim: Zimmer argues much of the prose's power comes from a technically skilled poet: Tom Bombadil's dialogue is in amphibrachs and amphimacers, galloping riders get dactylic and wolves spondaic stress patterns.
claims.source: Wikipedia, 'Poetry in The Lord of the Rings' (citing Zimmer)
claims.quote: written by a poet of high technical skill

claims.claim: Kullmann and Siepmann hold every poem follows a traditional genre and is fitted in style and content to its speaker, and Straubhaar that prose and verse are built to flow as an integrated whole.
claims.source: Wikipedia, 'Poetry in The Lord of the Rings'
claims.quote: fitted in style and contents to the characters

claims.claim: Kullmann argues the shift from prose to poetry directs attention from meaning to sound, with hobbit verse in simple iambic tetrameter, Elvish verse in liquid l-sounds, and Rohan's in Old English alliterative metre.
claims.source: Kullmann, 'Poetic Insertions in Tolkien's The Lord of the Rings', Connotations 23.2
claims.quote: direct the focus away from meaning to sound

claims.claim: Brauer observes that alliteration crosses from the Rohirrim's verse into the surrounding narrative prose of 'The Ride of the Rohirrim' (e.g. 'Fey he seemed').
claims.source: Gleaming Arch blog, 'Alliteration in The Return of the King' (David Brauer)
claims.quote: makes its way into Tolkien's prose

claims.claim: Thomas, using Booth's scale, finds The Hobbit opens with a very intrusive narrator who recedes as the book darkens, while LOTR's narrator is impartial and self-effacing and early LOTR drafts failed when they tried to return to the intrusive voice.
claims.source: kate_nepveu, 'LotR re-read: Thomas, Some of Tolkien's Narrators'
claims.quote: impartial and self-effacing

claims.claim: Litschko describes The Hobbit's narrator as an intrusive authorial narrator who comments on and judges characters, addresses readers directly, and carries a patronising quality suited to a young audience.
claims.source: Litschko, 'The Voice of the Narrator in J.R.R. Tolkien's The Hobbit' (2006, GRIN preview)
claims.quote: intrusive authorial narrator who frequently comments on and judges

claims.claim: Rateliff records that Tolkien's 1960 rewrite tried to bring The Hobbit into harmony with LOTR's mood, language and geography, and was abandoned because it was losing the humour and no longer read as The Hobbit.
claims.source: Wikipedia, 'The History of The Hobbit' (citing Rateliff, Fisher)
claims.quote: losing much of the humour

claims.claim: Furkó analyses discourse-pragmatic devices in The Hobbit as authentication strategies of its storytelling voice.
claims.source: Furkó 2020, 'Discourse Markers and Their Translation in Literary Discourse' (Springer chapter abstract)
claims.quote: authentication strategies

claims.claim: Kirk (1971), as summarised, treats LOTR as a philological experiment with a deliberate fairy-tale hobbit style, register graded by social standing (Frodo speaks more nobly), and a resistance to Latin-derived vocabulary.
claims.source: rogersdylan blog, 'I Would Rather Have Written in Elvish' (summary of Kirk 1971)
claims.quote: a grand philological experiment

claims.claim: Shippey describes The Silmarillion's compressed style, in which events are briefly documented as if in annals rather than told with novelistic attention to persons.
claims.source: Wikipedia, 'Tolkien's prose style' (citing Shippey 2005)
claims.quote: as if in annals

claims.claim: Bratman distinguishes four styles in the legendarium texts: Annalistic, Antique, Appendical and Philosophical.
claims.source: Wikipedia, 'Tolkien's Legendarium: Essays on The History of Middle-earth' (citing Bratman)
claims.quote: Annalistic, Antique, Appendical, and Philosophical

claims.claim: Turner's abstract holds The Silmarillion deliberately avoids conventional storytelling features to create a remote textworld that demands reader effort.
claims.source: Turner 2022, 'Style and Intertextual Echoes' (abstract via OpenAlex)

claims.claim: Shippey's 'impression of depth' arises from casual mentions of an untold background; Drout, Hitotsubashi and Scavera add that apparent contradictions between accounts give readers the impression of a real and complex history.
claims.source: Wikipedia, 'Impression of depth in The Lord of the Rings'
claims.quote: the impression of a real and complex history

claims.claim: The Red Book conceit, the Prologue's 'Note on the Shire Records' and the appendices produce an editorial distance mimicking historical recovery; West says the device appeals to the modern mystique of scholarly research.
claims.source: Wikipedia, 'Red Book of Westmarch'
claims.quote: the modern mystique of scholarly research

claims.claim: Flieger's Interrupted Music presents LOTR as one version of its story embodying references to other versions, with layered narrators, overlapping texts and variants that make the mythology read like a genuine tradition.
claims.source: Wikipedia, 'Interrupted Music'
claims.quote: multiple narrators, overlapping texts and variant versions

claims.claim: The interlaced narrative repeatedly leapfrogs between threads, limits the reader to what one Hobbit sees, and uses synchronising narrative landmarks to keep time shifts legible.
claims.source: Wikipedia, 'Interlacing in The Lord of the Rings'
claims.quote: narrative repeatedly leapfrogs

claims.claim: Agøy's survey of all descriptions in LOTR finds Tolkien's descriptions rarely very detailed, with characters, buildings and scenery described quite vaguely so readers complete the picture.
claims.source: Agøy 2013, 'Vague or Vivid? Descriptions in The Lord of the Rings', Tolkien Studies 10 (abstract via OpenAlex)
claims.quote: Tolkien's descriptions are rarely very detailed

claims.claim: Walker holds Tolkien's description sounds vividly detailed while actually giving an open-ended outline that lures readers into filling in the blanks.
claims.source: Tolkien Library interview with Steve Walker
claims.quote: lure us into filling in the blanks

claims.claim: Lee reports Rateliff's observation that Tolkien often describes a scene not as experienced but as remembered afterwards, and that Walker and Rateliff both call this the 'invitational style'.
claims.source: Lee 2022, close reading (ORA PDF), citing Rateliff 2009 and Walker 2009
claims.quote: as you would remember it afterwards

claims.claim: Walker credits the prose with a sense of time that brings past and future into the present; Shippey defends the Lament of the Rohirrim as a paraphrase of The Wanderer's ubi sunt against Manlove's charge of overworked cadences.
claims.source: Wikipedia, 'Literary reception of The Lord of the Rings' (and 'Tolkien's prose style')
claims.quote: overworked cadences

claims.claim: Reid's Hallidayan analysis of Theme/Subject in three tonally different excerpts finds shared grammar placing the discourses of mythology and history on a continuum that links LOTR to The Silmarillion.
claims.source: Reid 2009, 'Mythology and History: A Stylistic Analysis of The Lord of the Rings', Style 43.4 (abstract via Crossref)
claims.quote: considerably deeper and richer than critics have realized

claims.claim: Chen argues Tolkien's Secondary Belief is produced by a style of hypotyposis (vivid evocation), metalepsis and harmonism across LOTR and The Silmarillion.
claims.source: Chen 2014, 'Tolkien's Style of Fantasy', Caietele Echinox 26 (CEEOL abstract)
claims.quote: hypotyposis, metalepsis and harmonism

claims.claim: Livesey's keyness and collocation analysis tracks the Ring from a central to a peripheral place and from a magical to a burdensome device, registering a tonal fall from faerie to darkness across The Hobbit and LOTR.
claims.source: Livesey 2023, 'The Ring Cycle', Journal of Tolkien Research 18.1 (abstract)
claims.quote: gradual disenchantment of Tolkien's world

claims.claim: Moorcock's 'Epic Pooh' condemns the predominant tone as the prose of the nursery-room, a lullaby meant to soothe and console.
claims.source: Wikipedia, 'Literary reception of The Lord of the Rings'
claims.quote: the prose of the nursery-room

claims.claim: Edmund Wilson (1956) judged prose and verse alike professorially amateurish and the dialogue a story-book language out of Howard Pyle.
claims.source: Bookmarks, 'C. S. Lewis, W. H. Auden, & Edmund Wilson on The Lord of the Rings'
claims.quote: professorial amateurishness

claims.claim: Auden's 1954 review credits Tolkien with an amazing gift for naming and a wonderfully exact eye for description.
claims.source: LitHub, 'Read W. H. Auden's 1954 review of The Fellowship of the Ring'
claims.quote: wonderfully exact eye for description

claims.claim: Lewis's 1955 review praises the romance's very high architectural quality, its two-pattern six-book design, and the fact that no individual or species exists only for the plot.
claims.source: kate_nepveu, 'LotR re-read: Lewis, The Dethronement of Power'
claims.quote: very high architectural quality

claims.claim: Rateliff calls Tolkien a very careful stylist who weighed the effect of each word, against detractors such as Medcalf, who read sentences aloud to mock them, and Raffel.
claims.source: Rateliff, 'Tolkien's Style (Nobel, con't)' (Sacnoth's Scriptorium, 2012)
claims.quote: deliberately weighed the effect of each word

claims.claim: Lobdell argues the architecture and narrative style of the Edwardian adventure story (King Solomon's Mines, The Lost World) underlie The Hobbit and LOTR.
claims.source: Lobdell, The World of the Rings (Internet Archive record)
claims.quote: the Edwardian adventure story

claims.claim: Rosebury (as summarised on Wikipedia) shows the Witch-king passage starting in plain syntax and rising into a higher register when it touches ancient and magical history.
claims.source: Wikipedia, Tolkien's prose style (citing Rosebury 2003)

claims.claim: In the same passage Rosebury points to the inversion 'But glad would he have been' and assonance across blade/wield/dealt as deliberate elevation devices.
claims.source: Wikipedia, Tolkien's prose style (citing Rosebury 2003)
claims.quote: But glad would he have been

claims.claim: Tom Simon argues the narrative opens in a jolly Edwardian style, grows more serious as danger rises, and adopts definite formal archaism in the Rohan chapters.
claims.source: Tom Simon, The rhetoric of Middle-earth (Bondwine, 2013-01-11)
claims.quote: a jolly Edwardian style

claims.claim: Simon names Tolkien's mature register 'neo-archaic': archaic in tone and diction while carefully avoiding actual archaic words, with Aragorn the first major character to speak it.
claims.source: Tom Simon, The rhetoric of Middle-earth (Bondwine, 2013-01-11)
claims.quote: archaic in tone and diction

claims.claim: Once Aragorn enters, Simon says, the narrative's sentence structure itself begins to approximate an older diction rather than relying on antique words.
claims.source: Tom Simon, The rhetoric of Middle-earth (Bondwine, 2013-01-11)
claims.quote: begins to approximate an older diction

claims.claim: Simon defends archaic inversion by the 'Ask not / Don't ask' test: modernising the word order loses force and rhythm.
claims.source: Tom Simon, The rhetoric of Middle-earth (Bondwine, 2013-01-11)
claims.quote: loses force and rhythm

claims.claim: Simon argues that putting Théoden's speech about dying honourably into modern idiom would require an insincerity of thought, a disunion of word and meaning.
claims.source: Tom Simon, The rhetoric of Middle-earth (Bondwine, 2013-01-11)
claims.quote: a disunion of word and meaning

claims.claim: Simon reads the Old Forest chapters as sustained phantasmagoria, Bombadil's speech as loose metre, and the Amon Hen scene as a caesura separating the safer from the perilous half of the story.
claims.source: Tom Simon, The rhetoric of Middle-earth (Bondwine, 2013-01-11)
claims.quote: a kind of caesura

claims.claim: Simon's lesson for fantasy writers is that stylistic choices must serve the story and never call attention to themselves, or they bounce the reader out.
claims.source: Tom Simon, The rhetoric of Middle-earth (Bondwine, 2013-01-11)
claims.quote: bouncing one out of the story

claims.claim: Reviewing The Children of Húrin, Simon says Tolkien's signature trick is coupling archaic syntax with deliberately ordinary vocabulary.
claims.source: Tom Simon, The Children of Húrin review (Bondwine, 2007-05-19)
claims.quote: coupling archaic syntax with deliberately ordinary vocabulary
claims.page: The Children of Húrin, by J. R. R. Tolkien

claims.claim: Simon relays Tolkien's own defence that real archaic English is terser than modern English, illustrated by 'haply' carrying a whole clause of fatality.
claims.source: Tom Simon, The Children of Húrin review (Bondwine, 2007-05-19)
claims.quote: Real archaic English is far more terse than modern
claims.page: The Children of Húrin, by J. R. R. Tolkien

claims.claim: Simon describes the late Silmarillion prose as a cold and august style that cannot bend to everyday incident, whereas the early Lost Tales were vivid and immediate.
claims.source: Tom Simon, 1977: Lost tales, unattained vistas (Bondwine, 2007-03-16)
claims.quote: cold and august style

claims.claim: Simon argues The Silmarillion fails to give the reader a point of contact with the legendarium, the anchoring role hobbits perform in The Lord of the Rings.
claims.source: Tom Simon, 1977: Lost tales, unattained vistas (Bondwine, 2007-03-16)
claims.quote: a point of contact between the legendarium and the modern reader

claims.claim: Walker (per Wikipedia) finds truly archaic words like alas, thou, whither are rare; the antique feel comes from words such as deem, moot and wight rather than Old English.
claims.source: Wikipedia, Tolkien's prose style (citing Walker 2009)

claims.claim: Siepmann's corpus study attributes the impression of archaicity to three lexical causes: overuse of nineteenth-century fiction words, avoidance of modern-world words, and dense coinages, unusual grammar and rare words.
claims.source: Dirk Siepmann, Tolkien as a stylist: a corpus-based investigation (CL2017, Birmingham)
claims.quote: the avoidance of words associated with the modern world

claims.claim: Siepmann finds the key words shared with nineteenth-century novels cluster in landscape, position/direction (whither, thither, yonder, afar), warfare, and descriptive verbs, and were already obsolescent when Tolkien wrote.
claims.source: Dirk Siepmann, Tolkien as a stylist (CL2017)
claims.quote: obsolete or obsolescent at the time of writing

claims.claim: Siepmann shows Tolkien imports words from his own Beowulf translation (valour, valiant, corslet) and stretches them to new uses such as lightning that 'smote' the hills.
claims.source: Dirk Siepmann, Tolkien as a stylist (CL2017)
claims.quote: borrows a host of words from his translation of Beowulf

claims.feature: modern words in old grammatical patterns
claims.claim: Siepmann observes that Tolkien's modern key words are core vocabulary used in nineteenth-century patterns, e.g. 'smoke' with an indefinite article.
claims.source: Dirk Siepmann, Tolkien as a stylist (CL2017)
claims.quote: a black smoke swirled in the air

claims.claim: Siepmann notes a modernist trait in Tolkien's abundant descriptive verbs that carry an adverbial manner (clutch, cower, flicker, gleam, loom, peer, plod, stride).
claims.source: Dirk Siepmann, Tolkien as a stylist (CL2017)
claims.quote: abundant use of descriptive verbs

claims.claim: Words key only to The Lord of the Rings fall into warfare, natural features (dike, fen, dingle, starless), artefacts (fastness, sheath), peoples (lore-masters, wolf-riders), time (yesteryear) and prepositions (among, outwards), jointly producing an otherworldly atmosphere.
claims.source: Dirk Siepmann, Tolkien as a stylist (CL2017)
claims.quote: an atmosphere of medievalism or otherworldliness

claims.claim: Siepmann finds Tolkien prefers the homeliest collocations yet pairs everyday adjectives like 'great' unusually with abstractions, objects and weather, and leans on hyperbole domains (entire/maximum, loud, heavy, tall).
claims.source: Dirk Siepmann, Tolkien as a stylist (CL2017)
claims.quote: a marked preference for the most homely collocations available

claims.claim: Siepmann concludes Tolkien's prose deploys several centuries of English at once, putting old words to new uses and vice versa, making him a quiet linguistic postmodernist.
claims.source: Dirk Siepmann, Tolkien as a stylist (CL2017)
claims.quote: he is a linguistic postmodernist

claims.claim: Oakley Gordon argues the archaic quality of Tolkien's dialogue lies in word order rather than vocabulary, contrasting 'Nay, Gandalf!' with 'Not at all my dear G.' and calling the older orders terser and more vivid.
claims.source: Oakley Gordon, Language, Thought, and Worldviews in Tolkien's Writing (Salka Wind, 2021-12-24)
claims.quote: terser, more vivid
claims.page: Language, Thought, and Worldviews in Tolkien's Writing

claims.claim: Gordon relays Tolkien's point that a king who spoke in modern fashion would not have had those thoughts, so speech register encodes character and culture.
claims.source: Oakley Gordon, Salka Wind (2021-12-24)
claims.quote: would not have had those thoughts
claims.page: Language, Thought, and Worldviews in Tolkien's Writing

claims.claim: Ostadan, applying Le Guin, says Tolkien's elevated dialogue works by simple timelessness, the language of men of character, rather than fumbling with thee, thou and mayhap.
claims.source: Ostadan, From The Rings of Power to Poughkeepsie (TheOneRing.net, 2022-09-26)
claims.quote: the language of men of character
claims.page: From The Rings of Power to Poughkeepsie

claims.claim: Ostadan shows how modernisms such as 'Okay', 'like' and 'conflicted' dropped at random into otherwise timeless speech break the secondary world, the failure Le Guin's Poughkeepsie test detects.
claims.source: Ostadan, TheOneRing.net (2022-09-26)
claims.quote: at random in the midst of more timeless speech
claims.page: From The Rings of Power to Poughkeepsie

claims.claim: Le Guin's essay (per Wikipedia) holds that in fantasy every word counts and fantastic creation must reach into the words and grammar themselves, naming Tolkien among the writers who achieve it.
claims.source: Wikipedia, From Elfland to Poughkeepsie
claims.quote: fantastic creation should reach to the very words and grammar

claims.claim: Rateliff explains that Tolkien's thou marks familiarity (per Appendix F), so Éowyn's switch signals intimacy, but modern readers hear formality, an effect Tolkien aimed for and missed.
claims.source: John D. Rateliff, Eowyn's Thee and Thou (Sacnoth's Scriptorium, 2019-04-06)
claims.quote: Tolkien is trying for one effect and instead achieving another

claims.claim: Rateliff quotes Appendix F's note that Pippin used the familiar form to everyone in Minas Tirith, including Denethor, a comic register error Tolkien built in.
claims.source: John D. Rateliff, Sacnoth's Scriptorium (2019-04-06)
claims.quote: used the familiar for people of all ranks

claims.claim: Shippey (per Wikipedia) contrasts Aragorn's deceptively modern, easy-going range with Boromir's slightly wooden magniloquence, using speech to rank the two men.
claims.source: Wikipedia, The Council of Elrond (citing Shippey 2005)
claims.quote: slightly wooden magniloquence

claims.claim: Shippey reads the Gaffer's proverb-heavy talk, many words and few to the point, as the baseline of ordinary speech against which the other registers are measured.
claims.source: Wikipedia, The Council of Elrond (citing Shippey 2005)
claims.quote: many words and few to the point

claims.claim: Shippey notes Saruman, as quoted by Gandalf, talks like a politician in empty modern words (real, ultimate, deploring), the one modern register in the chapter.
claims.source: Wikipedia, The Council of Elrond (citing Shippey 2005)
claims.quote: talks like a politician

claims.claim: Shippey observes the Council chapter has twelve speakers plus seven more quoted inside Gandalf's monologue, which fills half the chapter, and succeeds as pure dialogue through register variation.
claims.source: Wikipedia, The Council of Elrond (citing Shippey 2005)

claims.claim: Meyer, following Shippey, finds Gandalf's speech only subtly archaized, mixing 'nigh' and 'mattered little' with modern idioms like 'for one thing'.
claims.source: Marguerite Meyer, Self-Stylin': Gandalf the Grey (Tolkien: Medieval and Modern, 2014-04-18)
claims.quote: subtly archaized

claims.claim: Meyer argues Gandalf is marked by versatility, moving from 'Ass! Fool!' to 'Thrice worthy and beloved' and reproducing seven other speakers' voices.
claims.source: Marguerite Meyer, Tolkien: Medieval and Modern (2014-04-18)
claims.quote: versatility and by the ability to hear and replicate other styles

claims.claim: Jaffe argues range of register marks adaptability: Aragorn moves between high and common styles, Elrond stays consistently archaic and formal, and Boromir has no range downward.
claims.source: David Jaffe, The Style of the Elf-Friend (Tolkien: Medieval and Modern, 2014-04-18)
claims.quote: consistently archaic and formal

claims.claim: The course blog tabulates the Council: Glóin in short broken sentences and apposition, hobbits in quick exclamations, Aragorn slipping between Elendil's heir and Strider, Boromir in a relatively Elrondian pattern.
claims.source: Tolkien: Medieval and Modern, Tolkien's Use of Poetry and Prose (2014-04-18)
claims.page: Tolkien's Use of Poetry and Prose

claims.claim: The same post describes the mature style as flexible, clear and simple, arrived at after early prose weighed down by sustained Morris-style archaism.
claims.source: Tolkien: Medieval and Modern (2014-04-18)
claims.quote: flexible, clear, simple
claims.page: Tolkien's Use of Poetry and Prose

claims.claim: The 2020 post shows Bilbo's 'Hullo!' chosen over 'hail', subject-dropped fragments like 'Feel ready for the great council?' marking informality, and Frodo's 'should like' marking moderate formality.
claims.source: Tolkien: Medieval and Modern, Hobbits at the Council of Elrond (2020-04-22)
claims.quote: Feel ready for the great council?
claims.page: Hobbits at the Council of Elrond

claims.claim: Kullmann and Siepmann (per Wikipedia) tabulate Aragorn as archaic and literary, Sam as colloquial, rustic, working class, Gandalf as plain and flexible, Pippin asking questions and Merry making direct statements.
claims.source: Wikipedia, Tolkien's prose style (citing Kullmann & Siepmann 2021)
claims.quote: colloquial, rustic, working class

claims.claim: Rosebury (per Wikipedia) identifies at least three orc dialects by rank, with Grishnákh talking like a melodrama villain or public-school bully and Gorbag in the idiom of a murderous bureaucracy.
claims.source: Wikipedia, Tolkien's prose style (citing Rosebury 2003)
claims.quote: like a melodrama villain, or a public-school bully

claims.claim: Vaninskaya (per Wikipedia) reads orc speech as twentieth-century soldier and functionary language, including the clipped telegraphese of 'Nazgûl uneasy. Spies feared on Stairs.'
claims.source: Wikipedia, Tolkien's prose style (citing Vaninskaya 2020)
claims.quote: clipped language of army dispatches

claims.claim: Rosebury calls Gollum's voice Tolkien's most memorable success: obsessive repetition, undeveloped syntax and unstable grammatical person suggesting mental illness.
claims.source: Wikipedia, Literary devices in The Lord of the Rings (citing Rosebury 2003)
claims.quote: obsessive repetition, undeveloped syntax and unstable grammatical person
claims.page: Literary devices in The Lord of the Rings

claims.claim: Milom's corpus study finds Gollum uses self-referent 'we/us' with non-standard verbs ('we doesn't') and sibilant reduplication mostly on plurals, while Sméagol keeps standard 'I' and grammar the closer he is to redemption.
claims.source: Vannessa L. Milom, Corpus Linguistic Analysis of the Idiolects of Gollum and Sméagol (J. Linguistics & Literature, 2022)
claims.quote: plural nouns were most likely to be injected with extra sibilants
claims.page: Corpus Linguistic Analysis of the Idiolects of Gollum and Sméagol

claims.claim: Shippey (per Wikipedia) says the Riders of Rohan are given Anglo-Saxon syntactic patterns and Old English words (éored, dwimmerlaik, mearas) to sound archaic, blunt and clear-sighted.
claims.source: Wikipedia, Tolkien's prose style (citing Shippey 2005)
claims.quote: Anglo-Saxon syntactic patterns

claims.claim: Shippey holds that the simple modern hobbit register mediates between the modern reader and the heroic, archaic registers of Elves, Dwarves and Rohirrim.
claims.source: Wikipedia, Literary devices in The Lord of the Rings (citing Shippey 2005)
claims.quote: mediate between the modern reader
claims.page: Literary devices in The Lord of the Rings

claims.claim: Turner (per Wikipedia) cites Pippin's 'O Wise People!' to Gildor as a hobbit attempting the formal register and thereby mediating it for the reader.
claims.source: Wikipedia, Tolkien's prose style (citing Turner 2020)
claims.quote: O Wise People!

claims.claim: Alaric Hall's lecture notes the Rohirrim speak the Old English dialect of Tolkien's own home region and that their verse alliterates on the stressed syllables in the Beowulf manner.
claims.source: Alaric Hall, Lord of the Rings lecture 4
claims.quote: alliteration of the stressed syllables

claims.claim: Hall says Tolkien absorbed the Beowulfian habit of layering different noun or verb phrases that denote one thing from several perspectives, while Beowulf still leaves more unsaid than Tolkien.
claims.source: Alaric Hall, Lord of the Rings lecture 4
claims.quote: layering of differing noun- or verb-phrases

claims.claim: Wilton lists revived Old English words (mathom, smial, barrow) and says Rohan's language was made to resemble ancient English so that its usages seem vaguely familiar and evoke ages past.
claims.source: David Wilton, Old English in LoTR (Wordorigins, 2020-03-07)
claims.quote: seem vaguely familiar and evoke images of ages past

claims.feature: ubi sunt echo of The Wanderer
claims.claim: Novelist Patricia Bracewell juxtaposes The Wanderer's ubi sunt formula with the Rohirrim lament to show Tolkien's prose carrying the current of Old English history and language.
claims.source: Patricia Bracewell, Tolkien and the Anglo-Saxons (2018-08-17)
claims.quote: the thrumming current of Old English history and language

claims.claim: The Universe in Words post shows the lament built on repeating a single phrase, 'Where is', each repetition conjuring one Rohirric image and conferring nostalgic value through rhetorical question.
claims.source: A Universe in Words, Tolkien, 'The Wanderer' and the Ubi Sunt-tradition (2015-11-07)
claims.quote: relies on the repetition of a single phrase
claims.page: Tolkien, 'The Wanderer' and the Ubi Sunt-tradition

claims.claim: Walker (per Wikipedia) reads the ubi sunt theme as producing an elegiac tone and a sense of deep time and history behind what can be seen.
claims.source: Wikipedia, Tolkien's prose style (citing Walker 2009)
claims.quote: deep time and history behind what can be seen

claims.claim: Drout (per Wikipedia) holds that the craftsmanship is consistent from the single sentence to the journey's macro-structure, all built on a repeated stress and release pattern.
claims.source: Wikipedia, Tolkien's prose style (citing Drout 2004)
claims.quote: a repeated stress and release pattern

claims.claim: Le Guin (as quoted by Nepveu) describes the whole narrative as a two-beat pattern of stress and release, inbreath and outbreath, walked at a human gait.
claims.source: kate_nepveu, LotR re-read: Le Guin, Rhythmic Pattern in The Lord of the Rings (2006-06-04)
claims.quote: Stress, release. Inbreath, outbreath. A heartbeat.

claims.claim: Le Guin grounds the book's rhythm in the irreducible simplicity of the trochaic beat and builds from it patterns of reversal (darkness/daylight, trap/freedom) in 'Fog on the Barrow-downs'.
claims.source: kate_nepveu on Le Guin (2006-06-04)
claims.quote: irreducible simplicity of the trochaic beat

claims.claim: Le Guin lists the devices by which the moral and physical world is built: repetition, semirepetition, suggestion, foreshadowing, recollection, echo and reversal.
claims.source: kate_nepveu on Le Guin (2006-06-04)
claims.quote: repetition, semirepetition, suggestion, foreshadowing, recollection, echo, and reversal

claims.claim: Le Guin (quoted by Fisher) says Tolkien's prose flows clearly and follows the breath, with punctuation exactly where a reader needs to pause, so it must be read aloud.
claims.source: Jason Fisher, Reading The Lord of the Rings aloud (Lingwë, 2010-09-23)
claims.quote: the cadences are graceful and inevitable
claims.page: Reading The Lord of the Rings aloud

claims.claim: Le Guin infers from the cadences that Tolkien must have heard what he wrote, placing him with Dickens and Woolf as writers whose narrative prose wants the living voice.
claims.source: Jason Fisher, Lingwë (2010-09-23)
claims.quote: Tolkien must have heard what he wrote
claims.page: Reading The Lord of the Rings aloud

claims.claim: Le Guin, in Conversations on Writing, says short rhythms repeated form long rhythms and this cyclical repetition is why the book enchants.
claims.source: Goodreads note, Ursula K. Le Guin: Conversations on Writing
claims.quote: Short rhythms repeated form long rhythms

claims.feature: iambic vs alliterative meter in prose
claims.claim: Venkatesh's writing lesson shows iambic pentameter driving plain action prose like a drumbeat, while elevated battle passages switch to four-stress Anglo-Saxon alliterative meter.
claims.source: Krishnan Venkatesh, Rhythm: A Writing Lesson from Tolkien (The Old Pearl Bed, 2017-01-13)
claims.quote: like a drumbeat, marking the relentless forward drive
claims.page: Rhythm: A Writing Lesson from Tolkien

claims.claim: Venkatesh says the alliterative sections turn incantatory and trance-like, with repetition ('All is lost. All is lost') intensifying emotion, and that double-meter lets Tolkien switch modes effortlessly.
claims.source: Krishnan Venkatesh, The Old Pearl Bed (2017-01-13)
claims.quote: incantatory, almost trance-like
claims.page: Rhythm: A Writing Lesson from Tolkien

claims.claim: McIntosh documents parataxis, short simple sentences joined by 'and', in the Ride of the Rohirrim and the Pelennor Fields, producing breathless excitement (citing Garth).
claims.source: Jonathan McIntosh, Tolkien's use of parataxis (The Flame Imperishable, 2012-03-22)
claims.quote: breathless excitement

claims.claim: Turner (per Wikipedia) shows the Pelennor 'and' chains in New Testament manner are stylistically marked, signalling an exalted register despite few archaic words.
claims.source: Wikipedia, Tolkien's prose style (citing Turner 2020)
claims.quote: stylistically marked

claims.claim: Shippey's term 'loose semantic fit' names Tolkien's deliberate use of conjunctions without explicit logical connection, evoking biblical narrative.
claims.source: Wikipedia, Tolkien's prose style (citing Shippey 2005)
claims.quote: loose semantic fit

claims.feature: verse embedded in prose at peaks
claims.claim: Shelton (per Wikipedia) notes Éomer declaims alliterative verse mid-battle, midway between lament and battle-cry, and the chapter closes on an elegiac lay imitating Beowulf.
claims.source: Wikipedia, Battle of the Pelennor Fields (citing Shelton; Mahon 1978)
claims.quote: Mourn not overmuch! Mighty was the fallen, meet was his ending

claims.claim: Mahon reads the Pelennor account as tinged with the elegiac, losses shadowing victory so the reader mourns while rejoicing.
claims.source: Wikipedia, Battle of the Pelennor Fields (citing Mahon 1978)
claims.quote: tinged with the elegiac

claims.claim: Walker finds Treebeard's lament obviously poetic in rhythm, and Forest-Hill and Dettmann find Tom Bombadil's speech essentially all in poetic metre.
claims.source: Wikipedia, Tolkien's prose style (citing Walker 2009; Forest-Hill 2015; Dettmann 2014)
claims.quote: essentially all in poetic metre

claims.claim: Drout criticises the fox passage in Fellowship as a failure of tone that drags the book back toward the intrusive Hobbit narrator, contrasting the successful 'if logs can be said to be contented'.
claims.source: Michael Drout, How to critique Tolkien's prose style (Wormtalk, 2007-04-12)
claims.quote: failure of tone
claims.page: How to critique Tolkien's prose style

claims.claim: Drout estimates more than half the novel is landscape description and asks whether the same effect could be won with fewer words.
claims.source: Michael Drout, Wormtalk (2007-04-12)
claims.quote: more than 50% of the novel
claims.page: How to critique Tolkien's prose style

claims.claim: Drout flags 'thrawn trees' as merely ornamental archaism with no descriptive job, while allowing 'grey falling curtains' because repetition layers it into an image.
claims.source: Michael Drout, Wormtalk (2007-04-12)
claims.quote: merely an ornamental archaism
claims.page: How to critique Tolkien's prose style

claims.claim: Drout praises 'Speeding along with little hope of stopping or turning' as an apo koinou construction that forces tiny re-readings of the sentence's meaning.
claims.source: Michael Drout, Wormtalk (2007-04-12)
claims.quote: Speeding along with little hope of stopping or turning
claims.page: How to critique Tolkien's prose style

claims.claim: Drout defends 'pinnacles or pillars of stone' as a calculated moment of reader confusion matching Frodo's uncertainty whether the forms are natural or carved.
claims.source: Michael Drout, Wormtalk (2007-04-12)
claims.page: How to critique Tolkien's prose style

claims.claim: Mambrol describes The Hobbit's narrator as intrusive and avuncular, addressing children with rhetorical questions, a style Tolkien later called bad.
claims.source: Nasrullah Mambrol, Analysis of Tolkien's The Hobbit (Literariness, 2021-02-18)
claims.quote: a bad style, as if one were talking to children

claims.claim: Litschko classifies The Hobbit's voice as an intrusive authorial narrator who comments, judges and guides, with a patronising quality and a shift of voice in the final chapters.
claims.source: Nadja Litschko, The Voice of the Narrator in J.R.R. Tolkien's The Hobbit (GRIN excerpt)
claims.quote: a somewhat patronising quality
claims.page: The Voice of the Narrator in The Hobbit

claims.claim: Bratman notes The Lord of the Rings begins like a fairy tale in domestic detail before widening into Germanic epic register and immense history.
claims.source: David Bratman, The History of Middle-earth (Tolkien Estate)
claims.quote: like a fairy tale
claims.page: David Bratman, The History of Middle-earth

claims.claim: Kirk (per Rogers) argues the fairy-tale 'Hobbit style' and the later shifts of narration are deliberate attempts to set the mood of each part of the tale.
claims.source: Dylan Rogers, I Would Rather Have Written in Elvish (2010-03-29, on Kirk 1971)
claims.quote: deliberate attempts to set the mood
claims.page: I Would Rather Have Written in Elvish

claims.claim: Bratman's taxonomy (per Wikipedia) divides the legendarium's prose into Annalistic, Antique, Appendical and Philosophical modes, and The Silmarillion's compressed annal-like style is what distances it from the novels.
claims.source: Wikipedia, The Silmarillion; Tolkien's Legendarium: Essays (citing Bratman 2000)
claims.quote: Annalistic, Antique and Appendical

claims.feature: depth via inconsistent documents in varied styles
claims.claim: Drout, Hitotsubashi and Scavera (per Wikipedia) trace the impression of depth to casual incomplete allusions and multiple inconsistent accounts written as if by different hands.
claims.source: Wikipedia, Impression of depth in The Lord of the Rings (citing Drout et al. 2014)
claims.quote: as if by different hands
claims.page: Impression of depth in The Lord of the Rings

claims.claim: Tolkien's Letter 247 (quoted on Wikipedia) locates the book's attraction in glimpses of a large history in the background, like a distant unvisited island.
claims.source: Wikipedia, Impression of depth in The Lord of the Rings (citing Tolkien Letter 247)
claims.quote: glimpses of a large history in the background
claims.page: Impression of depth in The Lord of the Rings

claims.claim: Sipahi (per Wikipedia) shows the Prologue frames the text as oral tradition written down, copied and redacted, so the narrator's voice is that of a translator-editor of old documents.
claims.source: Wikipedia, Impression of depth in The Lord of the Rings (citing Sipahi 2016)
claims.page: Impression of depth in The Lord of the Rings

claims.claim: Walker says Tolkien's description sounds vividly detailed but is an open-ended outline that invites readers to fill in the blanks, training wheels for the imagination.
claims.source: Interview with Steven C. Walker (Tolkien Library, 2009-07-22)
claims.quote: training wheels for our imagination

claims.claim: Walker (per Wikipedia) finds the prose strikingly invitational, relying on suggestion and semantic ambiguities that widen potential meaning.
claims.source: Wikipedia, Tolkien's prose style (citing Walker 2009)
claims.quote: semantic ambiguities tending to widen potential meaning

claims.claim: Auden's 1954 review credits Tolkien with an amazing gift for naming and an exact eye for description, judged by a realism stricter than Malory's age.
claims.source: W. H. Auden, The Hero Is a Hobbit (1954; Eighth Day Institute reprint)
claims.quote: amazing gift for naming and a wonderfully exact eye for description

claims.claim: Auden's 1956 review concedes light comedy is not Tolkien's forte and the opening chapters are a little shy-making, while the sense of the credible is never violated.
claims.source: W. H. Auden reviews (1954, 1956; Epistle of Dude reprint)
claims.quote: light comedy is not Mr. Tolkien's forte

claims.claim: Lewis's 1954 review says the names alone are a feast, sorted by sound into homely (Michel Delving), kingly (Boromir, Elendil) and loathsome (Gollum).
claims.source: C. S. Lewis, The Gods Return to Earth (1954; theonering.com reprint)
claims.quote: The names alone are a feast

claims.claim: Lewis characterises the book's register as gorgeous, eloquent and unashamed heroic romance, opening lighter in a way that risks losing readers.
claims.source: C. S. Lewis reviews (1954, 1955; Epistle of Dude reprint)
claims.quote: gorgeous, eloquent, and unashamed
claims.page: C.S. Lewis reviews The Lord of the Rings

claims.claim: Wikipedia's sound article reports Black Speech built to sound harsh with about 63% consonants and more voiced plosives against 52–55% for Elvish, which was chosen for beauty.
claims.source: Wikipedia, Sound and language in Middle-earth
claims.quote: to sound harsh

claims.claim: Tolkien's 1966 letter to Gene Wolfe, reprinted in Wolfe's essay, says he adopted 'warg' because it had a good sound for the meaning and derived 'orc' from Anglo-Saxon.
claims.source: Gene Wolfe, The Best Introduction to the Mountains (2001; scifiwright.com reprint)
claims.quote: had a good sound for the meaning
claims.page: The Best Introduction to the Mountains

claims.claim: Edmund Wilson's 1956 attack calls the prose storybook language out of Howard Pyle, with stereotyped characters and Sam talking lower-class and respectful.
claims.source: Edmund Wilson, Oo, Those Awful Orcs (1956; Epistle of Dude reprint)
claims.quote: Story-book language that might have come out of Howard Pyle

claims.claim: Wilson finds the terrors feeble and faceless, lacking concrete reality, and the episodes without development.
claims.source: Edmund Wilson, Oo, Those Awful Orcs (1956; Epistle of Dude reprint)
claims.quote: feeble and rather faceless

claims.claim: Moorcock's Epic Pooh calls high-fantasy prose the prose of the nursery-room, a lullaby and mouth-music enjoyed for its lack of tension.
claims.source: Michael Moorcock, Epic Pooh (1978; Arena 2 reprint PDF)
claims.quote: the prose of the nursery-room

claims.claim: Moorcock says the trilogy has many confused moments where the tension flags completely, yet concedes that at his best Tolkien writes better prose than his Oxford contemporaries.
claims.source: Michael Moorcock, Epic Pooh (1978; Arena 2 reprint PDF)
claims.quote: produce prose much better than that of his Oxford contemporaries

claims.claim: Wikipedia records Stimpson (1969) accusing Tolkien of wrenching syntax and shunning ordinary diction and Raffel (1968) rejecting the book partly on stylistic grounds.
claims.source: Wikipedia, Tolkien's prose style (citing Stimpson 1969; Raffel 1968)

claims.claim: La Porte's writing lesson shows Saruman's persuasion working through register: a gentle question, the tone of a kindly heart aggrieved, calling Théoden 'friend', each line building tension.
claims.source: Chris La Porte, Writing Compelling Dialogue and the Voice of Saruman (Porte Port, 2020-06-23)
claims.quote: of a kindly heart aggrieved

claims.feature: game design: slowness as Tolkien feel
claims.claim: Game designer Sage LaTorra argues The One Ring captures the feel of Tolkien's writing through deliberate length and slowness, its long-winded journeys and discourses, rather than mechanical elegance.
claims.source: Sage LaTorra, I Spent The Last Year Being A Hobbit (2021-07-12)
claims.quote: long-winded journeys
claims.page: I Spent The Last Year Being A Hobbit And Also Playing The One Ring

claims.claim: The Adventures in Middle-earth Loremaster's Guide (per its reviewer) tells game masters to keep the melancholic undertone of the long defeat, treating The Hobbit as a subjective memoir.
claims.source: rasmusnord01, Adventures in Middle-earth Loremaster's Guide review (Mindlands, 2017-10-23)
claims.quote: a melancholic undertone to Tolkien's world
claims.page: Adventures in Middle-Earth: Loremaster's Guide Review

claims.claim: The Return to Moria studio set as its first writing rule to use only Tolkien's actual words and avoid secondary interpretations, with Salo supplying Khuzdul dialogue.
claims.source: Return to Moria studio blog, Creating an Authentic Tolkien Journey (2024-07-03)
claims.quote: Only use Professor Tolkien's actual words.
claims.page: Blog: Creating an Authentic Tolkien Journey

claims.claim: Tauber's tokenisation gives The Hobbit about 95,137 tokens and 11,532 types, with just under half the types plain letter sequences and 291 hyphenated forms.
claims.source: James Tauber, Tokenizing the Hobbit (Digital Tolkien Project, 2021-03-14)
claims.quote: 95,137 tokens

claims.claim: Livesey's keyness and collocation study tracks the Ring's lexical field moving from magical to burdensome between The Hobbit and The Lord of the Rings.
claims.source: Michael Livesey, The Ring Cycle (Journal of Tolkien Research 18.1, 2023)
claims.quote: from a magical to a burdensome device

claims.claim: The Wikipedia article credits Drout (2004), not Le Guin, with the 'stress and release' formulation, while crediting Le Guin (2001) only with a sympathetic account of the style.
claims.source: Wikipedia, Tolkien's prose style

claims.claim: Tolkien rejects the 'tushery' charge, holding that genuine archaic English is terser than modern English and can say things the modern idiom cannot.
claims.source: Tolkien, Letter 171 to Hugh Brogan (1955), quoted in 'Passages I Highlighted in The Letters of J.R.R. Tolkien'
claims.quote: a real archaic English is far more terse than modern

claims.claim: Tolkien describes Théoden's dialogue as 'moderated or watered archaism', deliberately short of authentic Middle English while still non-modern.
claims.source: Tolkien, Letter 171, as quoted via Le Guin in TheOneRing.net, 'From The Rings of Power to Poughkeepsie'
claims.quote: moderated or watered archaism

claims.claim: Tolkien argues a king who spoke in modern idiom would not think the thoughts he expresses, so modernising the speech would create a disunion of word and meaning.
claims.source: Tolkien, Letter 171, quoted on LessWrong
claims.quote: an insincerity of thought, a disunion of word and meaning

claims.claim: Tolkien calls the belief that twentieth-century usage has special validity a delusion and tells his critic to shake off the parochialism of time.
claims.source: Tolkien, Letter 171, quoted in 'Tolkien on Machines, Power, Language, Love, War, and Everything Else'
claims.quote: shake yourself out of this parochialism of time

claims.claim: Tolkien insists 'argent' does not simply mean 'silver' and that a fine word should first be heard as sound in its poetic context.
claims.source: Tolkien, Letters, quoted on LessWrong
claims.quote: better to hear 'argent' as a sound only

claims.claim: Tolkien says the most moving effect is the sense of a vanished past and stories left untold rather than told.
claims.source: Tolkien, Letters, quoted on LessWrong
claims.quote: the untold stories that are most moving

claims.claim: Tolkien says he always begins writing from a name, and the name generates the story rather than the reverse.
claims.source: 1964 BBC interview with Denys Gueroult (broadcast 1971), transcript at Tolkien Library
claims.quote: give me a name and it produces a story

claims.claim: Tolkien defines hobbits as rustic English people made small, which grounds their plain modern speech register.
claims.source: BBC Radio 4 interview with Denys Gueroult, January 1971 broadcast, transcript at uv.es
claims.quote: Hobbits are just rustic English people

claims.claim: Tolkien says that once a story has several peoples on its hands the author must make them different from one another.
claims.source: BBC interview with Denys Gueroult, transcript at uv.es
claims.quote: you've got to make them different

claims.claim: Tolkien names Welsh style-and-sound and Finnish as the potent influences behind his nomenclature, especially mountain names.
claims.source: BBC interview with Denys Gueroult, transcript at uv.es
claims.quote: attracted me by it's style and sound

claims.claim: Tolkien says a complicated story must be worked to a map or it cannot be kept consistent.
claims.source: BBC interview with Denys Gueroult, transcript at uv.es
claims.quote: you must work to a map

claims.claim: Tolkien says everything he tried to write ahead of time proved no good and that the story grew without control.
claims.source: 1964 BBC interview reading notes
claims.quote: then it grew without control

claims.claim: Tolkien describes encountering a new language as like tasting a new wine, an aesthetic and nourishing pleasure underlying his invented tongues.
claims.source: Stuart D. Lee, ''Tolkien in Oxford' (BBC, 1968): A Reconstruction', Tolkien Studies 15 (ORA PDF)
claims.quote: just like tasting a new wine

claims.feature: laden familiar words for mythic furniture
claims.claim: Tolkien explains he used existing words like Dwarves, Elves and Middle-earth because mythic matter needs words already laden with sense, not everything strange at once.
claims.source: Stuart D. Lee, 'Tolkien in Oxford' reconstruction, Tolkien Studies 15
claims.quote: You can't have everything absolutely strange at the outright

claims.feature: engineered ugliness of the Black Speech
claims.claim: Tolkien states the Black Speech was designed to be hideous, and ranks sounds as pleasant or ugly by their place of articulation.
claims.source: Stuart D. Lee, 'Tolkien in Oxford' reconstruction, Tolkien Studies 15
claims.quote: It's a hideous language, it's meant to be hideous

claims.feature: no narrator asides / no talking down
claims.claim: Tolkien recalls that his children hated narrator asides and anything sounding like address to an audience, which taught him to drop that manner.
claims.source: 1968 BBC 'Tolkien in Oxford' interview transcript, Tolkien Library
claims.quote: They hated asides

claims.claim: Tolkien calls himself a natural niggler fascinated by detail who loves revision.
claims.source: Daphne Castell, 'The Realms of Tolkien', New Worlds, Nov 1966 (Fantastic Metropolis reprint)
claims.quote: I am a natural niggler, fascinated by detail

claims.claim: Tolkien says he takes special pride in readers who like his books for the names, and derides SF writers' childish name invention.
claims.source: Daphne Castell, 'The Realms of Tolkien', New Worlds, Nov 1966
claims.quote: praise of those who like my books for my names

claims.claim: Tolkien concedes The Hobbit caught sillinesses of manner unthinkingly from the children's-book convention.
claims.source: Tolkien, letter to W.H. Auden, 7 June 1955 (Letter 163), Tolkien Estate
claims.quote: sillinesses of manner caught unthinkingly

claims.claim: Tolkien tells Auden that languages and names are for him inseparable from the stories.
claims.source: Tolkien, letter to W.H. Auden, 7 June 1955 (Letter 163)
claims.quote: languages and names are for me inextricable from the stories

claims.feature: aesthetic pleasure in language for its own sake
claims.claim: Tolkien dates his craft to discovering the acute aesthetic pleasure derived from a language for its own sake.
claims.source: Tolkien, letter to W.H. Auden, 7 June 1955 (Letter 163)
claims.quote: acute aesthetic pleasure derived from a language for its own sake

claims.feature: dialectal style differentiation in translation frame
claims.claim: Tolkien explains he equated Westron with English and translated everything, but with differentiation of style to represent dialect, giving Gondor an antique style.
claims.source: Tolkien, Letter 144 to Naomi Mitchison (1954), reproduced at A Pilgrim in Narnia
claims.quote: some differentiation of style to represent dialectal differences

claims.claim: Tolkien says a good deal must remain unexplained even where explanation exists, because a mythical age needs enigmas.
claims.source: Tolkien, Letter 144 to Naomi Mitchison (1954)
claims.quote: even in a mythical Age there must be some enigmas

claims.claim: Tolkien states the invention of languages is the foundation and the stories were made to provide a world for the languages.
claims.source: Tolkien, Letter 165 to Houghton Mifflin (1955), quoted at Lingwë
claims.quote: To me a name comes first and the story follows

claims.feature: illusion of historicity via linguistic consistency
claims.claim: Tolkien holds that consistent invented language gives his work cohesion, a consistency of linguistic style and an illusion of historicity.
claims.source: Tolkien, Letters (165, 257) quoted in 'The Nature of Language', Tolkien: Medieval and Modern
claims.quote: a consistency of linguistic style, and an illusion of historicity

claims.claim: Tolkien says legends depend on their language and a living language equally on its legends, so an invented tongue needs a mythology.
claims.source: Tolkien, Letter 180 (1956), quoted on Wikiquote
claims.quote: Legends depend on the language to which they belong

claims.claim: Tolkien attributes the book's attraction to glimpses of a large history in the background, like a distant unvisited island or city in mist.
claims.source: Tolkien, Letter 247 (1963), quoted in Wikipedia 'Impression of depth in The Lord of the Rings'
claims.quote: glimpses of a large history in the background

claims.claim: Tolkien demands that characters' speeches be kept as he wrote them in style and sentiment, resenting their perversion more than plot changes.
claims.source: Tolkien, Letter 210 to Forrest Ackerman (1958), rec.arts.books.tolkien archive
claims.quote: in style and sentiment

claims.feature: tone must not be lowered to fairy-tale
claims.claim: Tolkien objects to phrases like 'Old scamp!' as lowering the tone toward a childish fairy-tale, and insists Gandalf must not splutter.
claims.source: Tolkien, Letter 210 to Forrest Ackerman (1958)
claims.quote: lower the tone towards that of a more childish fairy-tale

claims.claim: Tolkien insists the tale's peculiar tone rests on literal realism where miles, days and weather keep their real values.
claims.source: Tolkien, Letter 210 to Forrest Ackerman (1958)
claims.quote: miles are miles, days are days, and weather is weather

claims.feature: elvish enchantment / new names for new light
claims.claim: Tolkien describes trying to catch the air of timeless Elvish enchantment in Lothlórien, where Frodo's language has no names for what he sees.
claims.source: Dimitra Fimi, 'On Tolkien's Letter 131 (1): Capturing timeless Elvish enchantment'
claims.quote: the air of timeless Elvish enchantment

claims.claim: Tolkien planned to draw some great tales in full and leave many only placed in the scheme and sketched.
claims.source: Tea with Tolkien, 'Introduction to The Waldman Letter (Letter 131)'
claims.quote: leave many only placed in the scheme, and sketched

claims.claim: Tolkien prefers history, true or feigned, with its varied applicability, to allegory's authorial domination.
claims.source: Tolkien, Foreword to the Second Edition (1966), discussed at Tolkien's House of Being
claims.quote: history, true or feigned, with its varied applicability

claims.claim: Appendix F states that English in the book represents the Westron, with the whole linguistic setting translated into terms of our own times.
claims.source: Tolkien, Appendix F 'On Translation', discussed at TheOneRing.net Reading Room
claims.quote: translated as far as possible into terms of our own times

claims.feature: familiar vs deferential pronouns as register marker
claims.claim: Appendix F says Shire hobbits lost the familiar/deferential distinction, so Pippin addressed even Denethor familiarly, astonishing Gondor.
claims.source: John D. Rateliff, 'Eowyn's Thee and Thou' (Sacnoth's Scriptorium), quoting Appendix F footnote
claims.quote: including the Lord Denethor himself

claims.feature: degraded orc speech / elvish command of styles
claims.claim: Appendix F notes Elves commanded many styles while Orc and Troll speech was actually filthier than shown.
claims.source: Tolkien, Appendix F, discussed at TheOneRing.net Reading Room
claims.quote: more filthy than I have shown it

claims.claim: Tolkien represented the language of Rohan by the Mercian dialect of Old English within the English-for-Westron scheme.
claims.source: Wikipedia, 'Westron'
claims.quote: represented in this history by English

claims.claim: Tolkien says Common Speech names were crafted to be both translations and euphonious names of familiar English style, e.g. Rivendell for Imladris.
claims.source: Tolkien, 'Guide to the Names in The Lord of the Rings' (PDF)
claims.quote: a euphonious name of familiar English style

claims.feature: worn-down obsolete name-stock for the Shire
claims.claim: Tolkien explains Shire names carry elements that are obsolete, dialectal or worn-down in current English, giving them antiquarian texture.
claims.source: Tolkien, 'Guide to the Names in The Lord of the Rings'
claims.quote: obsolete or dialectal, or are worn-down and obscured in form

claims.claim: Tolkien identifies 'Oliphaunt' as an archaic form used as a rusticism, lamenting the loss of archaic colouring in translation.
claims.source: Tolkien, 'Guide to the Names in The Lord of the Rings'
claims.quote: an archaic form of 'elephant' used as a 'rusticism'

claims.claim: Tolkien prefers debased rustic associations of 'elf' over pretty literary fancies, signalling his distaste for ornamental register.
claims.source: Tolkien, 'Guide to the Names in The Lord of the Rings'
claims.quote: less damaging than the 'pretty' literary fancies

claims.feature: modernised Old English for Rohan names
claims.claim: Tolkien describes Rohan names such as Greyhame and Shadowfax as modernised or anglicised forms of Old English words.
claims.source: Tolkien, 'Guide to the Names in The Lord of the Rings'
claims.quote: Modernized form of Rohan grēg-hama

claims.claim: Tolkien argues Beowulf must be rendered in literary and traditional language because its diction was poetical, archaic and artificial in its own day.
claims.source: Wikipedia, 'On Translating Beowulf' (Tolkien, 1940)
claims.quote: poetical, archaic, artificial

claims.claim: Tolkien condemns colloquialism and false modernity, preferring 'striking' and 'smiting' to 'hitting' and 'whacking'.
claims.source: Wikipedia, 'On Translating Beowulf'
claims.quote: colloquialism and false modernity

claims.claim: Tolkien's rule for heroic diction is to avoid both the colloquial and the obscure, being antiquated without being arcane.
claims.source: Philip Irving Mitchell, 'Tolkien on Translating Beowulf' (DBU)
claims.quote: intentionally antiquated but not intentionally arcane

claims.claim: Tolkien holds that basic pleasure in the phonetic elements of a language is fundamental and prior to literary enjoyment, citing 'cellar door'.
claims.source: Tolkien, 'English and Welsh' (1955), quoted on Wikiquote
claims.quote: The basic pleasure in the phonetic elements of a language

claims.claim: Tolkien shows how a pleasing sound like 'cellar door' can become a name and then a character and situation.
claims.source: Anna Smol, 'Tolkien's cellar door'
claims.quote: from that a character, a situation begins to grow

claims.feature: elegiac annalist tone of The Silmarillion
claims.claim: Christopher Tolkien describes The Silmarillion's elegiac tone and long-age sweep, contrasting it with the narrative urgency of The Lord of the Rings.
claims.source: Christopher Tolkien, 'The Silmarillion', Tolkien Estate
claims.quote: things already old and weighted with regret

claims.claim: Le Guin says Tolkien writes plain clear English whose virtue is flexibility, ranging from commonplace to stately and sliding into verse unnoticed.
claims.source: Ursula K. Le Guin, 'From Elfland to Poughkeepsie' (1973), PDF
claims.quote: It ranges easily from the commonplace to the stately

claims.claim: Le Guin finds the Council of Elrond dialogue extraordinary for its simple timelessness, with sobriety, wit and force.
claims.source: Ursula K. Le Guin, 'From Elfland to Poughkeepsie'
claims.quote: an English extraordinary for its simple timelessness

claims.claim: Le Guin's test is to swap fantasy names for mundane ones; genuine fantasy dialogue survives because speech expresses character, as Boromir's slight whine shows.
claims.source: Ursula K. Le Guin, 'From Elfland to Poughkeepsie'
claims.quote: Speech expresses character.

claims.claim: Le Guin notes Tolkien's vocabulary is not striking and everything is direct, concrete and simple, with none of the fake-archaic 'ichor' register.
claims.source: Ursula K. Le Guin, 'From Elfland to Poughkeepsie'
claims.quote: he has no ichor

claims.claim: Le Guin warns the archaic manner is a perfect distancer only if done perfectly, and faults alternating slang with formal usage as breaking character coherence.
claims.source: Ursula K. Le Guin, 'From Elfland to Poughkeepsie'
claims.quote: It's a high wire: one slip spoils all.

claims.claim: Le Guin argues that in fantasy style is not an ingredient but the book itself, since every word counts where speech is creation.
claims.source: Ursula K. Le Guin, 'From Elfland to Poughkeepsie'
claims.quote: The style, of course, is the book.

claims.claim: Le Guin identifies a two-beat stress/release pulse, like breath or walking gait, as the fundamental rhythm carrying the whole narrative.
claims.source: Kate Nepveu, 'LotR re-read: Le Guin, Rhythmic Pattern in The Lord of the Rings'
claims.quote: Stress, release. Inbreath, outbreath.
