claims.feature: polar reversals at chapter and sentence scale
claims.claim: Le Guin traces reversals (darkness/daylight, trap/freedom) through 'Fog on the Barrow-downs' down to the chapter's final sentences.
claims.source: Kate Nepveu, 'LotR re-read: Le Guin, Rhythmic Pattern'
claims.quote: each yang contains its yin, each yin contains its yang

claims.claim: Le Guin observes each reversal recurs several times within a single chapter, making the pulsation structural rather than incidental.
claims.source: communicator, 'Le Guin on plot rhythm in Tolkein' (LiveJournal)
claims.quote: some three or four times

claims.claim: Shippey shows the Riders of Rohan given Anglo-Saxon syntactic patterns and stirring, alliteratively stately diction with words rescued from obscurity like 'éored'.
claims.source: Wikipedia, 'Tolkien's prose style' (citing Shippey and Walker)
claims.quote: stirring, alliteratively stately

claims.claim: Shippey names Tolkien's deliberate paratactic 'and' that avoids explicit logical connection 'loose semantic fit'.
claims.source: Wikipedia, 'Tolkien's prose style'
claims.quote: loose semantic fit

claims.claim: Shippey characterises The Silmarillion as documenting events as if in annals rather than as focused narrative.
claims.source: Wikipedia, 'Tolkien's prose style'
claims.quote: documented as if in annals

claims.feature: per-speaker register at the Council of Elrond
claims.claim: Shippey shows speakers at the Council distinguished by how they speak: Boromir 'Elrondian', Aragorn shifting register to impress him.
claims.source: 'J.R.R. Tolkien: Author of the Century, by Tom Shippey' (C.S. Lewis and J.R.R. Tolkien blog summary)
claims.quote: Boromir speaks sort of Elrondian

claims.claim: Shippey identifies The Hobbit's narrator voice in phrases like 'of course' and 'as you probably know' that treat the strange as obvious.
claims.source: 'Author of the Century' summary, C.S. Lewis and J.R.R. Tolkien blog
claims.quote: as you probably know

claims.claim: Shippey (as summarised) contrasts Glóin's and Gimli's curt, broken, appositive sentences with hobbits' simple rhymes and quick exclamations.
claims.source: 'Tolkien's Use of Poetry and Prose', Tolkien: Medieval and Modern
claims.quote: short, broken sentences and apposition

claims.claim: Aragorn slips between speaking as Elendil's heir and as Strider, marking rank and audience by register.
claims.source: 'Tolkien's Use of Poetry and Prose', Tolkien: Medieval and Modern
claims.quote: slips easily between speaking like Elendil's heir and Strider

claims.claim: Rosebury traces Tolkien's early sustained Morris-like archaism giving way to prose that shed impossibly heavy archaism.
claims.source: 'Tolkien's Use of Poetry and Prose', Tolkien: Medieval and Modern (citing Rosebury)
claims.quote: impossibly heavy archaism

claims.claim: Shippey explains hobbits serve as mediators between the modern reader's world and the heroic archaic realm, making the narrative accessible.
claims.source: Wikipedia, 'Storytelling in The Lord of the Rings'
claims.quote: mediators between the ordinary modern world

claims.claim: Shippey calls the impression of depth the one literary quality that most distinguishes Tolkien from his imitators.
claims.source: Wikipedia, 'Impression of depth in The Lord of the Rings'
claims.quote: most certainly distinguishes Tolkien from his many imitators

claims.feature: depth via varied hands and inconsistency
claims.claim: Drout and colleagues list four depth factors including casual incomplete mentions, inconsistent accounts, and varying textual styles as if by different hands.
claims.source: Wikipedia, 'Impression of depth in The Lord of the Rings'
claims.quote: varying textual styles as if written by different hands

claims.claim: Ferdynus notes characters constantly cite legends and recite old ballads, producing the impression of the depth of time.
claims.source: Wikipedia, 'Impression of depth in The Lord of the Rings'
claims.quote: the striking impression of the depth of time

claims.feature: plain phrasal verbs, not literary diction
claims.claim: Rosebury rebuts charges of archaising and wrenched syntax by showing Tolkien prefers 'have on' and 'get off' to 'wear' and 'dismount'.
claims.source: Wikipedia, 'Tolkien: A Cultural Phenomenon'
claims.quote: familiar phrasal verbs 'have on' and 'get off'

claims.claim: Rosebury credits Tolkien's description with a certain sensuous precision distinctive to him.
claims.source: Wikipedia, 'Tolkien: A Cultural Phenomenon'
claims.quote: a certain sensuous precision, distinctive of Tolkien

claims.claim: Rosebury shows passages begin in essentially plain syntax and rise to a higher register through subtle syntactic clues.
claims.source: Wikipedia, 'Tolkien's prose style'
claims.quote: essentially plain syntax

claims.claim: Rosebury holds the circumstantial expansiveness of Middle-earth itself is central to the work's aesthetic power.
claims.source: Wikipedia, 'Literary reception of The Lord of the Rings'
claims.quote: circumstantial expansiveness of Middle-earth itself is central

claims.claim: Walker says Tolkien's prose has an invitational quality, appearing detailed while luring readers to fill in the blanks like biblical prose.
claims.source: Tolkien Library, 'Interview with Steven C. Walker, author of The Power of Tolkien's Prose'
claims.quote: training wheels for our imagination

claims.claim: Walker finds the diction essentially nostalgic, even archaic, with the ubi sunt theme yielding an elegiac tone and feeling of deep time.
claims.source: Wikipedia, 'Tolkien's prose style' (citing Walker)
claims.quote: elegiac tone and a feeling of deep time and history

claims.claim: Walker describes the prose as taut with semantic ambiguities that widen potential meaning.
claims.source: Wikipedia, 'Tolkien's prose style' (citing Walker)
claims.quote: taut with semantic ambiguities tending to widen potential meaning

claims.claim: Turner finds Tolkien creating discrete linguistic registers for different characters, peoples and cultures, simple overall yet adapted to race and standing.
claims.source: Wikipedia, 'Tolkien's prose style' (citing Turner)
claims.quote: discrete linguistic registers for different characters, peoples, and cultures

claims.claim: Turner suggests embedding varied kinds of poem in prose came from William Morris, and hobbit verse echoes the rural Georgian poets.
claims.source: Wikipedia, 'Allan Turner'
claims.quote: markedly English and rural in character

claims.claim: Flieger describes the work's richness and multivalent texture that lets every reader take what they need.
claims.source: Wikipedia, 'Tolkien's prose style' (citing Flieger); Flieger interview at Tolkienista
claims.quote: so rich, so multi-valent

claims.feature: words and light as agents of perception
claims.claim: Flieger reads Tolkien through Barfield: language creates the reality it describes, with words and light as agents of perception splintered into many hues.
claims.source: Mythopoeic Society review of Flieger, 'Splintered Light'
claims.quote: language creates the reality it describes

claims.claim: Lewis praises the names as a feast that at moments embody a piercing, high, elvish beauty unmatched in prose.
claims.source: C.S. Lewis, 'The Gods Return to Earth' (Time and Tide, 1954), reproduced at TheOneRing.com
claims.quote: The names alone are a feast

claims.claim: Lewis says Middle-earth is heavier with its past than our world, so one cannot step anywhere without stirring the dust of history.
claims.source: C.S. Lewis, 'The Gods Return to Earth' (1954)
claims.quote: without stirring the dust of history

claims.claim: Lewis notes the book balances snug firesides and good cheer for the hobbit in each reader against great valour and anguish.
claims.source: C.S. Lewis, 'The Gods Return to Earth' (1954)
claims.quote: many a snug fireside and many an hour of good cheer

claims.claim: Lewis observes that much characterisation is done simply by making a figure an elf, dwarf or hobbit, and that the war has the quality of the war his generation knew.
claims.source: C.S. Lewis, 'The Dethronement of Power' (1955), reproduced at Earth and Oak
claims.quote: the very quality of the war my generation knew

claims.claim: Lewis singles out Treebeard, whose name would take too long to pronounce and who calls 'hill' a hasty word, as deep time embodied in speech.
claims.source: C.S. Lewis, 'The Dethronement of Power' (1955)
claims.quote: it would, by now, take too long to pronounce

claims.feature: gift for naming and exact description
claims.claim: Auden credits Tolkien with an amazing gift for naming and a wonderfully exact eye for description, in a northern saga-like landscape.
claims.source: W.H. Auden, 'The Hero Is a Hobbit' (NYT, 1954), reproduced at Epistle of Dude
claims.quote: a wonderfully exact eye for description

claims.feature: historical and social reality within Quest
claims.claim: Auden says Tolkien uses the Quest's traditional properties while satisfying our sense of historical and social reality.
claims.source: W.H. Auden, 'At the End of the Quest, Victory' (NYT, 1956), at Anthropology of Accord
claims.quote: satisfying our sense of historical and social reality

claims.claim: Auden judges the opening hobbit comedy weak, saying light comedy is not Tolkien's forte.
claims.source: Biblioklept, 'W.H. Auden Reviews J.R.R. Tolkien'
claims.quote: light comedy is not Mr. Tolkien's forte

claims.claim: Edmund Wilson attacks the prose as professorial amateurishness with characters talking a Howard Pyle story-book language.
claims.source: Book Marks, 'C. S. Lewis, W. H. Auden, & Edmund Wilson on The Lord of the Rings'
claims.quote: professorial amateurishness

claims.feature: hostile: class snobbery in speech; overworked cadences
claims.claim: Stimpson reads character language as class snobbery and Manlove hears overworked cadences and monotonous pitch, hostile readings Shippey and Rosebury rebut.
claims.source: Wikipedia, 'Literary reception of The Lord of the Rings'
claims.quote: overworked cadences

claims.feature: corpus: three lexical causes of archaicity
claims.claim: Siepmann's corpus study finds the impression of archaicity comes from overuse of nineteenth-century fiction words, avoidance of modern-world words, and dense rare or obsolescent words.
claims.source: Dirk Siepmann, 'Tolkien as a stylist: a corpus-based investigation into The Lord of the Rings' (Corpus Linguistics 2017, Birmingham)
claims.quote: the avoidance of words associated with the modern world

claims.feature: corpus: nineteenth-century key words in four sets
claims.claim: Siepmann finds dense nineteenth-century key words in landscape, position/direction (whither, thither, yonder, afar), warfare, and descriptive verbs and adjectives.
claims.source: Dirk Siepmann, 'Tolkien as a stylist' (2017)
claims.quote: obsolete or obsolescent at the time of writing

claims.claim: Siepmann shows Tolkien borrows words from his own Beowulf translation (valour, valiant, corslet) and stretches them to new uses like 'lightning smote'.
claims.source: Dirk Siepmann, 'Tolkien as a stylist' (2017)
claims.quote: borrows a host of words from his translation of Beowulf

claims.feature: corpus: modern words in nineteenth-century patterns; descriptive verbs
claims.claim: Siepmann finds modern core words used in nineteenth-century patterns ('a black smoke') and an abundance of manner-laden descriptive verbs like gleam, loom, plod and stride.
claims.source: Dirk Siepmann, 'Tolkien as a stylist' (2017)
claims.quote: use many of these words in nineteenth-century patterns

claims.feature: corpus: dialogue share and hobbit viewpoint
claims.claim: Kullmann and Siepmann find about half the book is dialogue, verse or embedded story, and narrative adopts the hobbits' viewpoint about 85% of the time.
claims.source: Wikipedia, 'Storytelling in The Lord of the Rings' (citing Kullmann & Siepmann 2021)
claims.quote: About half of The Lord of the Rings consists of dialogue

claims.feature: non-standard speech marks Sam and Gollum; epic style for heroes
claims.claim: Kullmann and Siepmann note Sam and Gollum are marked by non-standard speech while omniscient passages shift to epic style marking Aragorn as an old-style hero.
claims.source: Wikipedia, 'Tolkien's prose style' and 'Storytelling in The Lord of the Rings' (citing Kullmann & Siepmann)
claims.quote: marked out by their non-standard speech

claims.claim: Kullmann and Siepmann's book treats key words and collocations, narrative syntax, points of view, landscape, speeches, storytelling, poems, and language and character as separate stylistic systems.
claims.source: Google Books, 'Tolkien as a Literary Artist' (Kullmann & Siepmann, 2021)
claims.quote: The Narrative Syntax of The Lord of the Rings

claims.claim: Robbins argues Tolkien's phonology and phonaesthetics were applied directly to the various English prose styles of the book, not only to invented languages.
claims.source: Susan Robbins, 'Beauty in Language: Tolkien's Phonology and Phonaesthetics...' (CEEOL abstract)
claims.quote: the various prose styles of English used in writing

claims.claim: Halbrooks shows the narrator's voice changing with setting, cheerful near the Shire and later sounding like an historian, nature writer or epic poet.
claims.source: John Halbrooks, 'Tolkienian Style'
claims.quote: like an historian, or a nature writer, or an epic poet

claims.claim: Halbrooks reads 'Concerning Hobbits' as nineteenth-century antiquarianism and Gandalf's tale as paratactic clause-chaining seeded with unfamiliar proper nouns.
claims.source: John Halbrooks, 'Tolkienian Style'
claims.quote: paratactic movement from clause to clause

claims.claim: Strider talks colloquially with hobbits but switches to high speech with Boromir, and Elrond's antiquity comes from vocabulary plus inverted grammar.
claims.source: 'Sublimis and Humilis; Aragorn and Strider', Tolkien: Medieval and Modern
claims.quote: a combination of both vocabulary and grammar

claims.claim: Rateliff argues Éowyn's shift to thee/thou marks intimacy, a poetic-diction register modern readers have lost and misread as formality.
claims.source: John D. Rateliff, 'Eowyn's Thee and Thou' (Sacnoth's Scriptorium)
claims.quote: we've lost 'poetic diction'

claims.claim: Bowman notes the Red Book device puts the tale inside quotation marks, casting Tolkien as translator rather than author.
claims.source: Wikipedia, 'Storytelling in The Lord of the Rings'
claims.quote: inside quotation marks

claims.claim: Forchhammer's analysis of narrative layers includes stylistic shifts between high or epic passages and down-to-earth narration within the chronicler frame.
claims.source: alt.fan.tolkien thread 'Narrative voice examples (LotR)'
claims.quote: down to earth

claims.feature: Shippey on delivered archaism and metre
claims.claim: Shippey remarks that Tolkien's lines are archaic though persuasive when delivered with conviction, and that Tolkien became very strict about metre.
claims.source: Writers Write, 'Talking LOTR With Tolkien Expert Professor Thomas Shippey'; Tolkien Library Shippey chat
claims.quote: archaic though they often are

claims.claim: The LotR narrator's voice shifts with circumstance and with which characters are present, from the comic fox aside in the Shire to darker, unsettling prose once the hobbits leave it.
claims.source: John Halbrooks, Tolkienian Style (Substack, 2024-03-13)
claims.quote: A fox passing through the wood on business of his own

claims.claim: Gandalf's telling of Isildur's death uses paratactic clause structure and unfamiliar proper nouns to sound sombre and chronicle-like.
claims.source: John Halbrooks, Tolkienian Style
claims.quote: He leaped into the waters, but the Ring slipped

claims.claim: The Prologue's subtitle 'Concerning Hobbits' adopts a nineteenth-century antiquarian register, and the early chapters carry more place-names than The Hobbit to signal expansion.
claims.source: John Halbrooks, Tolkienian Style
claims.quote: Concerning Hobbits

claims.feature: register shift Book IV to Book V
claims.claim: The prose rises from hobbit-colloquial in Book Four to a heroic register in the Pelennor chapters of Book Five.
claims.source: John Halbrooks, Heroic Language in The Lord of the Rings (Substack, 2026-08-12)
claims.page: Heroic Language in The Lord of the Rings
claims.quote: the hosts of Mordor wailed, and terror took them

claims.claim: After Théoden's four-stress alliterative verse, the narration itself takes on the alliterating prose rhythm of Old English writers like Ælfric and Wulfstan, resonating with the preceding verse.
claims.source: John Halbrooks, Heroic Language in The Lord of the Rings
claims.page: Heroic Language in The Lord of the Rings
claims.quote: Fey he seemed, or the battle-fury of his fathers

claims.claim: No speaker at the Council answers in the same manner of speech as the previous one; Elrond stays consistently archaic and formal while Aragorn code-switches between Strider's plain style and his high style.
claims.source: Jaffe, The Style of the Elf-Friend (Tolkien: Medieval and Modern, 2014)
claims.quote: whose style is consistently archaic and formal

claims.claim: Glóin is characterised as curt through short, broken sentences, and each people's syntax marks its culture; alliterative verse and heroic-style prose become interchangeable when matched in register.
claims.source: MCS, Tolkien's Use of Poetry and Prose (Tolkien: Medieval and Modern, 2014-04-18)
claims.page: Tolkien's Use of Poetry and Prose
claims.quote: short, broken sentences

claims.feature: iambic base shifting to alliterative metre
claims.claim: Tolkien's martial prose runs on an iambic foundation and shifts into Old English alliterative metre at the ecstatic climax of the Rohirrim's charge; the horn passage scans in both metres at once.
claims.source: Krishnan Venkatesh, Rhythm: A Writing Lesson from Tolkien (2017-01-13)
claims.page: Rhythm: A Writing Lesson from Tolkien
claims.quote: With that he seized a great horn from Guthláf

claims.claim: The horn-blast passage and the Rohan songs follow Anglo-Saxon alliterative patterns, so that Rohan's prose emulates Beowulf.
claims.source: David Brauer, Alliteration in The Return of the King (Gleaming Arch, 2014-09-07)
claims.page: Alliteration in The Return of the King
claims.quote: With that he seized a great horn

claims.claim: Tolkien's prose is almost entirely one-syllable native English words, preferring English coinages such as 'unlooked-for' to Latinate 'unexpectedly'.
claims.source: Mark, Goodreads discussion: Tolkien's prose, what makes it so vigorous?
claims.page: Tolkien's prose: what makes it so vigorous?
claims.quote: unlooked-for instead of unexpectedly

claims.claim: Tolkien's tempo is slow but never plodding, he changes mode and register seamlessly, and fast epic passages are deliberately limited so they contrast with the surrounding prose.
claims.source: Alun Ephraim, cellar door (Substack, 2023-09-03)
claims.quote: His tempo was typically slow, but never plodding.

claims.claim: A long sentence tracks difficult movement and short sentences then supply details; the Barrow-downs and Dead Marshes rely on word-sound, alliteration and understated rhyme.
claims.source: Alun Ephraim, cellar door
claims.quote: alliteration, an understated bit of rhyme

claims.claim: The Silmarillion mixes distinct Annalistic, Antique and Appendical styles with alliterating words and rhythmical prose (citing Nagy).
claims.source: Galin, Planet Tolkien forum: Writing style/turns of phrase
claims.quote: Annalistic, Antique, and the Appendical

claims.claim: Tolkien writes plain, clear English whose outstanding virtue is flexibility, ranging from the commonplace to the stately and sliding into metre in the Bombadil episode unnoticed; his vocabulary is not striking and has no ichor.
claims.source: Ursula K. Le Guin, From Elfland to Poughkeepsie (1973)
claims.quote: ranges easily from the commonplace to the stately

claims.claim: The Aragorn/Boromir/Elrond exchange is an English extraordinary for its simple timelessness that could not be mistaken for Capitol Hill, and Boromir's slight whine is characterising.
claims.source: Ursula K. Le Guin, From Elfland to Poughkeepsie (1973)
claims.quote: an English extraordinary for its simple timelessness

claims.claim: Le Guin's judgement that Tolkien's plain English is direct, concrete and simple is quoted and endorsed by a language blogger.
claims.source: Stan Carey, Sentence first (2024-10-16)
claims.page: 'How to see one's own world': Ursula K. Le Guin on writing style
claims.quote: no ichor; everything is direct, concrete and simple

claims.claim: Auden credits Tolkien with an amazing gift for naming and an exact eye for description that make the reader know the world like their own childhood.
claims.source: W. H. Auden, 1954 review (LitHub reprint)
claims.page: W. H. Auden's 1954 review of The Fellowship of the Ring
claims.quote: a wonderfully exact eye for description

claims.feature: names as prose beauty; historical density
claims.claim: Lewis calls the names a feast embodying piercing elvish beauty and says one cannot set foot anywhere without stirring the dust of history.
claims.source: C. S. Lewis, The Gods Return to Earth (TheOneRing reprint)
claims.quote: The names alone are a feast

claims.claim: Tolkien selects registers to suit peoples: simple and modern for hobbits, more archaic for Dwarves, Elves and Rohirrim, with hobbits mediating for the modern reader (Turner).
claims.source: Wikipedia, Tolkien's prose style
claims.quote: simple and modern for Hobbits

claims.claim: Shippey shows Elrond speaking with antique words and old-fashioned syntactic inversions while the hobbits speak modern English.
claims.source: Wikipedia, Tolkien's prose style (Shippey)
claims.quote: Now, therefore, things shall be openly spoken

claims.claim: Shippey reads Saruman's vocabulary as empty politician-speak built on words like 'real' and 'ultimate'.
claims.source: Wikipedia, Tolkien's prose style (Shippey)
claims.quote: we can bide our time, we can keep

claims.claim: Walker finds only a handful of genuinely archaic words, used rarely, yet the diction seems in essence nostalgic; the Riders of Rohan get Anglo-Saxon syntactic patterns and stately alliterative diction.
claims.source: Wikipedia, Tolkien's prose style (Walker)
claims.quote: stirring, alliteratively stately

claims.claim: The repeated 'and' in the New Testament manner is stylistically marked, signalling something extraordinary (Turner/Shippey).
claims.source: Wikipedia, Tolkien's prose style
claims.quote: And then wonder took him

claims.claim: Rosebury answers Stimpson by showing that even her chosen example is as plain as Hemingway, and that the Merry/Witch-king passage begins plainly then modulates to a higher register for ancient history.
claims.source: Wikipedia, Tolkien's prose style (Rosebury)
claims.quote: And still Meriadoc stood there blinking

claims.claim: Drout holds that the craftsmanship is consistent from the individual sentence to the macro-structure of the journey as a repeated stress-and-release pattern.
claims.source: Wikipedia, Tolkien's prose style (Drout)
claims.quote: repeated stress and release pattern

claims.claim: Walker's book argues the prose is strikingly invitational, taut with semantic ambiguity that widens meaning and draws the reader into sub-creation.
claims.source: Wikipedia, Tolkien's prose style (Walker)
claims.quote: strikingly invitational

claims.claim: The ubi sunt theme gives elegiac tone and historical depth, as when Pippin guesses at great men and kindreds from the ruins.
claims.source: Wikipedia, Tolkien's prose style (Walker)
claims.quote: Pippin guessed of great men and kindreds

claims.claim: The impression of depth is built from offhand, incomplete references to the past, multiple inconsistent accounts as in real history, and different texts written in different styles.
claims.source: Wikipedia, Impression of depth in The Lord of the Rings
claims.page: Impression of depth in The Lord of the Rings
claims.quote: from the Hoard of Scatha the Worm

claims.claim: Turner notes archaising object-fronting such as 'Weapons they have laid at your doors', which German can keep but French cannot render.
claims.source: Wikipedia, Translating The Lord of the Rings (Turner)
claims.page: Translating The Lord of the Rings
claims.quote: Weapons they have laid at your doors

claims.claim: Sam and the Gaffer use double negatives, subject duplication and altered agreement, while Gollum's idiolect has ungrammatical syntax and plurals like 'pocketses'.
claims.source: Wikipedia, Translating The Lord of the Rings (Bayona)
claims.page: Translating The Lord of the Rings
claims.quote: Mr. Drogo, he married...

claims.claim: Kullmann and Siepmann find about 85% of narrative time focalized through the four hobbits, with character viewpoint conveying state of mind while omniscient narration stays vivid; the epic style is archaic diction plus parataxis linked by 'and'.
claims.source: Wikipedia, Storytelling in The Lord of the Rings (Kullmann/Siepmann)
claims.page: Storytelling in The Lord of the Rings
claims.quote: parataxis with clauses linked with 'and'

claims.claim: The corpus study finds the impression of archaicity comes from overuse of nineteenth-century-fiction words, avoidance of modern-world words, and dense coinages, unusual grammar and obsolescent words, across four lexical sets (landscape, direction, warfare, descriptive verbs).
claims.source: Dirk Siepmann, Tolkien as a stylist: a corpus-based investigation (Birmingham CL2017)
claims.page: Tolkien as a stylist: a corpus-based investigation into The Lord of the Rings
claims.quote: three simple lexical causes

claims.claim: Tolkien borrows words from his Beowulf translation (valour, valiant, corslet) and uses modern core words in nineteenth-century patterns such as 'a black smoke', alongside modernist manner-laden verbs (cower, flicker, loom, plod).
claims.source: Dirk Siepmann, Tolkien as a stylist (Birmingham CL2017)
claims.quote: Branched lightning smote down upon the eastward hills

claims.claim: Tolkien prefers the most homely collocations available but attaches 'great' unusually densely to peril, trees, halls, gates, clouds and shadow, and key semantic domains point to hyperbole.
claims.source: Dirk Siepmann, Tolkien as a stylist (Birmingham CL2017)
claims.quote: marked preference for the most homely collocations

claims.claim: Shippey observes that Boromir speaks 'sort of Elrondian' and that Aragorn adopts that register to Boromir to impress him, so character shows in how they say things.
claims.source: C.S. Lewis and J.R.R. Tolkien blog, review of Author of the Century
claims.page: J. R. R. Tolkien: Author of the Century, by Tom Shippey
claims.quote: Boromir speaks sort of Elrondian

claims.claim: Shippey notes The Hobbit's narration see-saws between Bilbo's 'business manner', the narrator's matter-of-fact tone and Thorin's high style, with 'of course' and 'as you probably know' hinting at hidden depths.
claims.source: C.S. Lewis and J.R.R. Tolkien blog, review of Author of the Century
claims.page: J. R. R. Tolkien: Author of the Century, by Tom Shippey
claims.quote: business manner

claims.claim: Shippey uses the Council of Elrond to show how language and register shifts bring out differences in status and character.
claims.source: Danny Yee, review of Shippey (2022)
claims.page: Tom Shippey: The Road to Middle-Earth; Author of the Century
claims.quote: bring out differences in status and character

claims.claim: Théoden's 'Nay, Gandalf!' speech uses only words still current; its archaism is in the sentence arrangement, and the final clause order carries a thought modern idiom cannot (quoting Letter 171).
claims.source: Oakley Gordon, Language, Thought, and Worldviews in Tolkien's Writing (Salka Wind, 2021-12-24)
claims.page: Language, Thought, and Worldviews in Tolkien's Writing
claims.quote: terser, more vivid, and sometimes nobler than modern English

claims.claim: Letter 171 rejects 'tushery', calls real archaic English far terser than modern, and shows that rewriting Théoden into modern idiom produces a disunion of word and meaning because his thoughts are themselves archaic.
claims.source: Tolkien Gateway, Letter 171
claims.quote: much terser and more vivid ancient style

claims.feature: syntax and morphology do the work
claims.claim: Citing Shippey, Alden argues Tolkien's vocabulary is not obsolete; the archaic mood comes from Early Modern English syntax (OSV fronting) and inflection (-eth, thou/ye), and in the Silmarillion Elves use thou almost always, noble Men less, common Men never.
claims.source: Sparrow F. Alden, Early Modern English Inflectional Morphology (Mythmoot II, 2013)
claims.page: Early Modern English Inflectional Morphology: Not Just Another Pretty Spreadsheet
claims.quote: But the Palantir the king will keep

claims.claim: In the Athrabeth Finrod moves deliberately between formal 'you' and intimate 'thou' to open and close distance with Andreth, encoding relationship in grammar.
claims.source: Sparrow F. Alden, Early Modern English Inflectional Morphology (Mythmoot II, 2013)
claims.quote: Finrod uses the different inflections to connote

claims.claim: Éowyn's shift to thee/thou with Aragorn was meant as intimacy but modern readers hear formality; Appendix F admits the familiar/deferential distinction is impossible to represent and was hinted by inconsistent 'thou'.
claims.source: John D. Rateliff, Eowyn's Thee and Thou (Sacnoth's Scriptorium, 2019-04-06)
claims.quote: inconsistent use of thou

claims.claim: Mythgard forum posters treat thee/thou in the Silmarillion as the familiar form that nonetheless sounds formal today, note Yea/Nay as the cheap archaism, and grade the Valar most archaic with First-Age Elves one step down.
claims.source: Mythgard Forums, Modern Turns of Phrase and Archaic Language (2019)
claims.page: Modern Turns of Phrase and Archaic Language | Page 2
claims.quote: Yea/Nay for Yes/No

claims.claim: Citing Garth, McIntosh shows chains of 'and' clauses at the Pelennor ('and he was still unscathed, and he was young, and he was king') crank up tension and elevate Théoden to a god of old.
claims.source: Jonathan McIntosh, Tolkien's use of parataxis (The Flame Imperishable, 2012-03-22)
claims.quote: and he was still unscathed, and he was young

claims.claim: Nepveu singles out the opening sentences of the chapter's last paragraph, whose repeated 'but he outpaced it / but he was ever before them' convey momentum.
claims.source: Kate Nepveu, LotR re-read: The Ride of the Rohirrim (2010-05-07)
claims.page: LotR re-read: Return of the King V.5, The Ride of the Rohirrim
claims.quote: but he was ever before them

claims.feature: comma withheld for pace; spearpoint ending
claims.claim: Commenters on the Grey Havens re-read note that Tolkien left 'a far green country' without a comma so as not to slow the prose, and that 'Well, I'm back' works as a spearpoint driven home by everything before it.
claims.source: Kate Nepveu, LotR re-read: The Grey Havens (2011-01-13) and comments
claims.page: LotR re-read: Return of the King VI.9, The Grey Havens
claims.quote: didn't want to slow down his prose with a comma

claims.claim: Wormtongue's 'pale wise face' exploits the older non-positive sense of 'wise', 'froward tongue' is King James Proverbs diction, and Tolkien changed 'fire and flood' to 'fire and death' to remove ambiguity.
claims.source: Kate Nepveu, LotR re-read: The King of the Golden Hall, and comments
claims.page: LotR re-read: Two Towers III.6, The King of the Golden Hall
claims.quote: a pale wise face and heavy-lidded eyes

claims.claim: Le Guin's close reading of 'Fog on the Barrow-downs' finds a two-beat rhythm of stress and release, with the chapter's final plain sentences full of rapid reversals that fall like drumbeats in quiet simple language.
claims.source: Kate Nepveu, LotR re-read: Fog on the Barrow-downs (quoting Le Guin's Rhythmic Pattern)
claims.page: LotR re-read: Fellowship I.8, Fog on the Barrow-downs
claims.quote: They are like drumbeats.

claims.claim: The omniscient narrator reappears on the Downs to raise and simultaneously discount supernatural possibility, calling the standing stone 'more like a warning'.
claims.source: Kate Nepveu, LotR re-read: Fog on the Barrow-downs
claims.page: LotR re-read: Fellowship I.8, Fog on the Barrow-downs
claims.quote: more like a warning

claims.feature: depths of time in a chapter
claims.claim: Dunharrow's Púkel-men and the Baldor episode make 'The Muster of Rohan' a chapter full of history and the depths of time, seen through Merry's wonder and pity.
claims.source: Kate Nepveu, LotR re-read: The Muster of Rohan
claims.page: LotR re-read: Return of the King V.3, The Muster of Rohan
claims.quote: the depths of time

claims.claim: Le Guin's essay, as summarised, reads the narrative as pulsing between polarities (darkness/daylight, confusion/clarity, imprisonment/freedom), each reversal recurring three or four times per chapter, and hears a Beethoven finale when the closing lines are read aloud.
claims.source: Kate Nepveu, LotR re-read: Le Guin, Rhythmic Pattern in The Lord of the Rings (LiveJournal)
claims.page: LotR re-read: Le Guin, Rhythmic Pattern in The Lord of the Rings
claims.quote: Stress, release. Inbreath, outbreath. A heartbeat.

claims.claim: Le Guin (2001, quoted by Fisher) says even long sentences flow clearly and follow the breath, punctuation falls where one needs to pause, the cadences are graceful and inevitable, and the prose wants the living voice.
claims.source: Jason Fisher, Reading The Lord of the Rings aloud (Lingwë, 2010-09-23)
claims.page: Reading The Lord of the Rings aloud
claims.quote: the cadences are graceful and inevitable

claims.claim: In the Barrow-downs the prose moves from heavy heat to wet fog to sudden violence as the mist is 'rolled up and thrust aside', with conflicting sensations that make even the stars ominous.
claims.source: Katie, LotR Re-Read: Fog on the Barrow Downs (The Fandomentals, 2016-05-11)
claims.page: Lord of the Rings Re-Read: Fog on the Barrow Downs
claims.quote: the mist was rolled up and thrust aside

claims.feature: simple short sentences at high drama
claims.claim: The Cirith Ungol escape pairs drama with a simplicity of prose: short plain sentences such as 'There was a crack.' and 'Then they ran.'
claims.source: Katie, The Tower of Cirith Ungol (The Fandomentals, 2018-09-12)
claims.quote: pairs nicely with a simplicity of prose

claims.feature: free indirect discourse in crisis; Gothic register
claims.claim: Frodo's temptation in the barrow is rendered in free indirect discourse, and the grave-goods details give the chapter a Gothic antiquarian register distinct from the novel's vernacular voice.
claims.source: Abigail Nussbaum, The Great Tolkien Reread: Fog on the Barrow-Downs (2026-03-10)
claims.page: The Great Tolkien Reread: Fog on the Barrow-Downs
claims.quote: He thought of himself running free over the grass

claims.claim: 'In a hole in the ground there lived a hobbit' runs on three-syllable feet with the iamb 'there lived' acting as an invisible colon and the last foot inverting the rhythm, while the hole is described by negation.
claims.source: John Sanders, Of Feet and Hobbit-Holes (Broadly Textual, 2019-10-15)
claims.page: Of Feet and Hobbit-Holes: Lessons Learned from a Literary Intro
claims.quote: not a nasty, dirty, wet hole

claims.claim: The Hobbit's first sentence is a portal of words whose two-to-three-word units are successive steps of entry, withholding the definition of 'hole' until context reframes it.
claims.source: Shawn Marchese, Down the Hobbit Hole (Prancing Pony Ponderings, 2017-09-17)
claims.quote: a portal of words

claims.claim: The Hobbit's narrator comments and converses with the reader in an avuncular, almost condescending voice Tolkien later called a bad style and dropped for the uncommenting omniscience of LotR.
claims.source: Nasrullah Mambrol, Analysis of Tolkien's The Hobbit (Literariness, 2021-02-18)
claims.quote: well, you will see

claims.claim: The LotR narrator is less explicit than The Hobbit's but still present in offhand foreknowledge and poetic interludes, and the hobbit viewpoint is held whenever a hobbit is on stage.
claims.source: Evan Þ, Narrators and Perspectives (Papyrus Rampant, 2023-10-07)
claims.quote: the narrator's voice isn't as explicit

claims.claim: Forum readers hear The Hobbit's narrator as a parent's bedtime voice that softens the blow of deaths, unlike LotR's sparser narration.
claims.source: Forumshire thread on narrative voice in The Hobbit
claims.page: How do you feel about the use of narrative voice in The Hobbit
claims.quote: softens the blow

claims.claim: 'No living man am I' opens with negation then affirmation, 'Éowyn I am, Éomund's daughter' is a pre-duel self-naming challenge, and the closing conditional is parallel and archaic.
claims.source: middle-earth-mythopoeia (Tumblr)
claims.page: The movie dialogue could never measure up to this
claims.quote: Éowyn I am, Éomund's daughter

claims.claim: 'Where now the horse and the rider?' adapts the Wanderer's ubi sunt lament, rephrasing its opening question and expanding it item by item.
claims.source: M.E. Bond, Tolkien's Influences: The Wanderer (2019-05-27)
claims.quote: Where now the horse and the rider?

claims.claim: The Rohan lament is a recognisable ubi sunt, a lament for greatness past and irrecoverable built on rhetorical questions.
claims.source: Anglophilic Anglican, Ubi sunt? Song of the Rohirrim (2019-07-30)
claims.page: Ubi sunt? – Song of the Rohirrim: a lament
claims.quote: a well-known poetic form

claims.claim: Tolkien turns the Old English 'Hwær cwom mearg?' into an expanded meditation running through rider, horn, helm, hauberk, harp and harvest.
claims.source: Lucy Holland, where is the horse and the rider (Silvan Historian, 2025-02-23)
claims.page: where is the horse and the rider

claims.claim: Nearly all alliterative verse in LotR belongs to the Rohirrim; it front-loads stress on consonant clusters rather than end-rhyme, and the prose following 'Arise, arise' is full of battle-fury.
claims.source: Ross Cawthon, #4 Arise, Alliteration! (Medium, 2022-06-22)
claims.quote: frontloads the rhyming stress

claims.claim: Usenet readers, citing Petty and Rosebury via Hammond and Scull, describe the Ainulindalë's highly formal King James-style diction with -eth forms as scriptural yet distinctively Tolkien's.
claims.source: alt.fan.tolkien, Analysis and Criticism of the Ainulindale (narkive)
claims.page: Analysis and Criticism of the Ainulindale
claims.quote: the fire that giveth Life and Reality

claims.claim: The Valaquenta opens 'in the beginning' and the Ainulindalë proclaims Eru 'one', echoing Genesis and Deuteronomy in diction.
claims.source: Douglas Estes, Tolkien and the Bible (Bible Odyssey)
claims.quote: in the beginning

claims.claim: Old English greetings and revived words (Westu Théoden hál, dwimmerlaik, mathom, smial) are dropped into Rohirric speech and hobbit vocabulary.
claims.source: David Wilton, Old English in LoTR (Wordorigins)
claims.quote: Westu Théoden hál

claims.claim: The gate and door challenges at Edoras are the book's most direct Beowulf homage, and the chapter opens with accumulated temporal description.
claims.source: Michael Halila, Let's Read Tolkien 47: The King of the Golden Hall (2018-08-06)
claims.page: Let's Read Tolkien 47: The King of the Golden Hall
claims.quote: They rode on through sunset, and slow dusk

claims.claim: Walker says Tolkien's essential stylistic tactic is to lure readers into filling in the blanks, giving an open-ended outline that sounds vividly detailed.
claims.source: Steve Walker interview (Tolkien Library, 2009-07-22)
claims.quote: lure us into filling in the blanks

claims.claim: A commenter reads Théoden's 'Hail the victorious dead' as about as Anglo-Saxon as one can get without being at Maldon.
claims.source: Patrick Nielsen Hayden, comment on Reactor (2021)
claims.page: Actually, Théoden Has the Best Dialogue in The Lord of the Rings
claims.quote: Hail the victorious dead

claims.claim: The Grey Havens closes on emotional restraint, with Sam's 'Well, I'm back' as the hobbit response to epic events.
claims.source: Never Felt Better, Chapter by Chapter: The Grey Havens (2012-03-08)
claims.page: The Lords Of The Rings, Chapter By Chapter: The Grey Havens
claims.quote: Well, I'm back

0.trueWording: modulating into a higher register to deal with the echoes
0.note: Substance confirmed: 'Tolkien begins this in plain language, modulating into a higher register to deal with the echoes of ancient and magical history,' attributed to Rosebury. NOT verbatim: the claim's quote drops the definite article ('with echoes' vs 'with the echoes'). Also note the page says 'plain language', not 'plain modern language', and asserts no 'only where' exclusivity.

1.trueWording: discrete linguistic registers for different characters, peoples, and cultures
1.note: Exact string present in the rendered article: 'Turner states that The Lord of the Rings makes use of several styles of prose, with discrete linguistic registers for different characters, peoples, and cultures.' The Hobbit/Dwarf/Elf/Rohirrim contrast follows in the same sentence group. Caveat: the page cites this to Turner 2013 (pp. 545-546), not Turner 2020/2022 as the claim's source line states; Turner 2020 is cited elsewhere for a different point.

2.trueWording: are on their way to becoming a means of distinguishing
2.note: OpenAlex record confirms Allan Turner, 'Style and Intertextual Echoes', 2022, correct DOI. Abstract (reconstructed from the inverted index) reads 'Stylistic features are on their way to becoming a means of distinguishing between different characters and different cultural and ethical outlooks' and 'Tolkien was able to achieve local and temporal color by including a high proportion of intertextual references to older literatures.' The claim drops the abstract's hedge, asserting features 'become' rather than 'are on their way to becoming'.

3.trueWording: Hobbits serve as mediators between the modern world and fantasy realm
3.note: Page: 'Shippey explains that the Hobbits serve as mediators between the ordinary modern world and the heroic and archaic fantasy realm, making The Hobbit and The Lord of the Rings readily accessible,' cited to Shippey 2005 p. 259 — matching the claim's stated source. Wording differs: 'ordinary modern world' not 'modern reader', and 'fantasy realm' not 'world of the epic'. No quote was offered, so verbatim status is not at issue.

4.trueWording: Shippey argues Tolkien does an extraordinary job
4.note: Page supports the length and the all-talk character: readers 'may dismiss it as a waste of fifteen thousand words because there is little to no action, other than people conversing back and forth,' and Shippey credits Tolkien's 'integration of cultural variation' (Shippey 68-69), with distinct voices demonstrated for Elrond, Gloin, Boromir and Aragorn. But 'tour de force' appears nowhere on the page (zero occurrences); the essay's phrase is 'does an extraordinary job'. That framing is the claim's own.

5.trueWording: Isildur's scroll, more so than Elrond, uses old -eth endings
5.note: The page assigns the -eth examples to the wrong party relative to the claim. It reads: 'Isildur's scroll also displays archaism, more so than Elrond, utilizing the "old -eth verb endings - 'seemeth', 'fadeth'"' — explicitly distinguishing Isildur from, and ranking him above, Elrond on exactly the cited feature. The quoted fragment 'old -eth verb endings' is present but describes Isildur's scroll, not Elrond's speech. Separately, 'inverted constructions' is attributed on this page to Boromir, and 'signalling his great age' does not appear. Only the general point that Elrond's archaism runs 'in terms of grammar and vocabulary' is supported here.

6.trueWording: achieved not just by vocabulary ... but also by grammar
6.note: The page quotes Shippey directly: '...Elrond's archaism is consistent, achieved not just by vocabulary (the first resort of the amateur medievalist), but also by grammar' (p. 76). Both fragments on either side of the claim's ellipsis appear word for word, and the ellipsis honestly marks the elided parenthetical. Attribution to Shippey and the consistency point both check out.

7.trueWording: Gloin is curt: short, broken sentences and apposition (Shippey, 71)
7.note: The quoted phrase is verbatim, but the scholar is wrong. The page reads 'Gloin (and by extension dwarves) is curt, which readers in our primary reality know by his use of short, broken sentences and apposition (Shippey, 71)' — credited to Shippey p. 71, not Rosebury. Rosebury is cited on this page only at pp. 91, 95 and 117, all for Tolkien's early and evolving style (romantic imitations, Morris-like archaism, the mature 'intimate paternal story-telling' voice), never for dwarvish speech. The parallel Wix source likewise credits Gloin's taciturnity to Shippey (p. 70).

8.note: Exact match in context: 'Boromir is most closely associated with Elrondian, utilizing "inverted constructions," whereas Aragorn is more colloquial (72-73).' Both halves of the claim — Boromir's proximity to Elrond's idiom and Aragorn's colloquialism in the same Council scene — are directly supported.

9.trueWording: His manner of speech changes directly with the situation
9.note: Exact sentence present, continuing '...and represents the dual nature of Aragorn and Strider.' The colloquial-among-hobbits and formal-in-high-settings halves are both borne out ('Around the hobbits... can talk very colloquially'; 'when presented with a formal situation, Aragorn can quickly switch'). Minor caveat: the compound term 'sermo humilis' does not appear; the essay quotes Auerbach's Mimesis as 'the low style was sermo remissus or humilis' against 'sermo gravis or sublimis', and explicitly parallels Aragorn's high/low contrast to it.

10.trueWording: politically minded, abstract manners of speech
10.note: Exact match: 'Saruman's duplicity can be felt through his politically minded, abstract manners of speech.' Caveat on the claim's paraphrase and its 'modern idiom' feature label: the page does not describe Saruman's speech as modern — that adjective is the claim's addition, and this page's modernity discussion attaches to other characters.

11.note: Exact match: 'Tolkien even went to far as to consider the tone and cadence with which the Rohirrim would speak C.S.; it being their second language, he imagined it would be much slower and more deliberate.' Both the second-language reason and the Common Speech referent are explicit. Caveat: this sentence is not itself tied to the Tiller letter on the page — the letter to Terrence Tiller is cited two sentences later for a different quotation (on 'linguistic differentiation... in diction, idiom', p. 254).
